meta.blurb: Two strangers praise Solomon Northup's violin and offer him paid work. He is a free man from New York. Then he wakes in chains. It will take twelve years, and one honest carpenter, to bring him home.
meta.bible: Solomon Northup: born free in Minerva, New York, in July 1808; a farmer, a carpenter and a Violin player; kidnapped in Washington in 1841 and held as a slave for twelve years; freed in January 1853; the author of the book, published in 1853. Mintus Northup: his father, born into slavery and freed on the death of his master; died in 1829. Anne Hampton: his wife, married on Christmas Day 1829. Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo: their three children. Brown and Hamilton: the two men who tricked him with a promise of work as a musician. James Burch: the slave dealer who held him in Washington. Eliza: a woman held with him, with her children Emily and Randall. Theophilus Freeman: the slave dealer of New Orleans, who called him Platt. William Ford: a Baptist preacher and kind master in the Pine Woods of Louisiana. John Tibeats: a cruel carpenter. Chapin: Ford's overseer, who saved him. Edwin Epps: a harsh cotton planter at Bayou Boeuf, Louisiana, who held him for about ten years. Mary Epps: his wife. Patsey: the best cotton picker on Epps's plantation. Armsby: a poor white labourer who betrayed him. Samuel Bass: a Canadian carpenter, an opponent of slavery, who wrote the letters that saved him. Henry B Northup: the New York lawyer, from the family that once owned Solomon's father, who came to find him. Washington Hunt: the governor of New York. Judge Turner: the judge at Marksville. David Wilson: the New York writer who helped him to write the book. William Henry Harrison: the President whose funeral Solomon saw in April 1841. Places: Minerva, Saratoga Springs, Sandy Hill, New York, Washington, the Capitol, Richmond, Virginia, New Orleans, Louisiana, Red River, Pine Woods, Bayou Boeuf, Marksville, Georgia, Canada. Key terms: Slavery, Overseer, Plantation, Cotton, Sugar cane, Violin, Mortgage, Abolition, Kidnapping, Brig, Steamboat, Swamp, Bayou, Hunt. Voice and tone: serious, dignified and clear; cruelty is stated plainly and briefly, never graphically; the writer respects Solomon Northup's courage and quotes nothing from his book at length. Added for the full-length book. Ebenezer Radburn: Burch's jailer in Washington. Robert and Arthur: two men held with Solomon in Richmond and on the brig Orleans; they spoke of seizing the ship, and Robert died of smallpox at sea. Randall and Emily: Eliza's children; Randall was sold first, and Emily was kept back when Eliza left with Ford. Peter Tanner: Ford's brother-in-law, a hard master for whom Solomon worked for a time. Uncle Abram, Aunt Phebe and Wiley: others held on Epps's plantation. Parker and Perry: Saratoga merchants who knew Solomon and received Bass's letter. John P Waddill: the Marksville lawyer who helped Henry B Northup. Harriet Beecher Stowe: author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, to whom the book is dedicated. Samuel Bass: a Canadian carpenter who worked at Marksville and argued with Epps that slavery was wrong. Dates: the funeral of Harrison was on 10 April 1841; Henry B Northup reached Epps's cotton field on 3 January 1853; Solomon was sold to Epps in about 1843. Marksville is the seat of Avoyelles Parish. In Washington a Black witness could not testify against a white man; the case against Burch failed, and none of the kidnappers was ever convicted.

A Name Called Across a Field

beats.scene: A man in a plain coat sits at a table with papers
beats.summary: Solomon Northup's book of 1853 is the true account of a free man who was stolen from his family and kept as a slave for twelve years.

beats.scene: A small farm in the New York hills with a wooden house
beats.summary: Solomon is born free in Minerva, New York, in July 1808; his father Mintus had been a slave.

beats.scene: An old man reads a paper at a table while a young Mintus watches
beats.summary: Mintus belonged to a family named Northup and was freed by his master's will.

beats.scene: A father teaches a boy to read beside a violin on the wall
beats.summary: Mintus teaches his son to read, write and farm, which was unusual for a Black family of that time.

beats.scene: A boy plays a violin in a farm kitchen while neighbours dance
beats.summary: As a boy Solomon falls in love with the violin and soon plays at village dances.

beats.scene: A young man steers a timber raft along a canal
beats.summary: As a young man Solomon works on the Champlain Canal, steering rafts of timber, and once travels as far as Canada.

beats.scene: A young couple stand together outside a farmhouse on a winter day
beats.summary: After his father dies in 1829, Solomon marries Anne Hampton on Christmas Day.

beats.scene: A young family stands in a farmyard: two girls and a small boy
beats.summary: The couple farm near Fort Edward and Anne becomes known as a cook; their three children are Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo.

beats.scene: A busy hotel in a New York spa town, guests arriving
beats.summary: In 1834 the family moves to Saratoga Springs, where Solomon works at hotels and on building jobs and Anne cooks.

beats.scene: A tidy house on a village street, three children at the door
beats.summary: By spring 1841 Solomon is thirty-two, with a home, steady work and many friends, and no idea that it is about to end.

beats.scene: Two well-dressed men speak warmly with a smiling Solomon on a street
beats.summary: In late March 1841 two strangers calling themselves Brown and Hamilton praise his violin playing.

beats.scene: Two men lean across an inn table, coins and a map between them
beats.summary: They say they belong to a circus that needs a musician in Washington, and offer a dollar a day and three dollars for each show.

beats.scene: A man hesitates in a doorway holding a travelling bag and a coat
beats.summary: Anne and the children are away for the spring, and Solomon, tempted by the pay, decides to go, expecting to be back in a few weeks.

beats.scene: A carriage leaves Saratoga with three men aboard
beats.summary: Solomon packs a few clothes and sets off with the two men by carriage for Albany.

beats.scene: A steamboat on the Hudson River arrives at crowded New York docks
beats.summary: From Albany they travel down the Hudson to New York City, where the two men treat Solomon with great kindness.

beats.scene: A clerk writes at a high desk while Solomon waits, hat in hand
beats.summary: On Brown's suggestion Solomon obtains at the New York Custom House an official paper proving that he is a free man.

beats.scene: A train crosses open countryside in spring with passengers at the windows
beats.summary: By ferry and railway through New Jersey, Philadelphia and Baltimore they travel south to Washington.

beats.scene: A hotel on a broad avenue hung with black cloth for mourning
beats.summary: They reach Washington while the city mourns President Harrison, take rooms at a hotel, and pay Solomon part of his wages in advance.

beats.scene: A man walks beside the white Capitol dome in the evening light
beats.summary: While waiting for the circus Solomon walks about the capital and admires the Capitol, where slavery was still lawful.

beats.scene: A long funeral procession passes along a wide avenue in the capital
beats.summary: On 10 April 1841 Solomon watches the great funeral procession of President Harrison.

beats.scene: A man lies sick in a hotel bed while two shadowy figures stand by
beats.summary: After supper Solomon is taken very ill, remembers only pain and strange faces, and later believes that his wine was drugged.

beats.scene: A man sits alone in chains on a stone floor in a dark cell
beats.summary: Solomon wakes in a dark cell, in chains, with his money and free papers gone.

beats.scene: A barred window lets a thin grey light fall on an empty bench
beats.summary: Alone in the dark, Solomon cannot believe that Brown and Hamilton, who had been so kind, have vanished.

beats.scene: Two men stand in a cell doorway, one of them holding a heavy paddle
beats.summary: The slave dealer James Burch tells him he is a runaway from Georgia named Platt; Solomon replies that he is a free man from New York.

beats.scene: A broken wooden paddle lies on a stone floor beside a coiled whip
beats.summary: Because Solomon keeps saying that he is free, Burch and the jailer Ebenezer Radburn beat him, first with a paddle that breaks, then with a whip.

beats.scene: A bruised man lies on a cell floor in pale light
beats.summary: Burch warns that if Solomon ever says again that he is free he will be killed; Solomon learns that the truth has become the most dangerous thing he can say.

beats.scene: A high-walled yard with the Capitol dome rising white above it
beats.summary: By day the captives are let into a yard behind high walls, from which Solomon can see the dome of the Capitol.

beats.scene: Men and women sit close together on the floor of a crowded dim room
beats.summary: Many of those held in the pen are waiting to be sent south and sold; they speak quietly of families left behind.

beats.scene: A woman cries beside two small children in a crowded dim room
beats.summary: He meets Eliza and her two children, Emily and Randall, who are also to be sold; Eliza cannot stop weeping.

beats.scene: A man lies awake at night, staring at a small barred window
beats.summary: In the long nights Solomon thinks of Anne and the children and looks for some way to send word, but he has no paper, no pen and no one to trust.

beats.scene: Guards lead chained captives from the pen into a dark street at night
beats.summary: One night Burch has the captives taken out in chains and driven through the dark streets of Washington to the river.

beats.scene: A steamboat on a dark river with chained captives on the lower deck
beats.summary: A steamboat carries them down the Potomac in the night; the other passengers do not notice, or do not care.

beats.scene: A train rushes through woods and farms with a plain car of chained people
beats.summary: From the river a train carries them on to Richmond, and again the travellers around them take no notice.

beats.scene: A high-walled yard in a southern city, people sitting on the ground
beats.summary: In Richmond, Virginia, they are held in another slave pen; the city was one of the largest centres of the slave trade.

beats.scene: Two men whisper together in a crowded pen at night
beats.summary: In the Richmond pen Solomon meets two men, Robert and Arthur, who tell him that they too were once free.

beats.scene: A large sailing ship at anchor in a harbour, captives boarding in chains
beats.summary: From Richmond the brig Orleans carries them towards New Orleans, the captives sleeping below deck in chains.

beats.scene: Three men whisper beside a ship's wooden wall in the dark
beats.summary: Solomon, Robert and Arthur plan to seize the ship and sail for a free place.

beats.scene: A sick man lies in a dark ship's hold, a lantern nearby
beats.summary: Smallpox breaks out on the ship; Robert falls ill, then Solomon.

beats.scene: Sailors lower a wrapped body into a grey sea
beats.summary: Robert dies and is buried at sea; Solomon recovers slowly, and the plan to seize the ship dies with his friend.

beats.scene: A ship sails up a wide brown river towards a city
beats.summary: The brig enters the Mississippi and comes up the river to New Orleans, one of the biggest slave markets in the country.

beats.scene: Chained captives walk from a ship along a busy wharf past cotton bales
beats.summary: The captives are marched from the wharf to the slave pen of the dealer Theophilus Freeman.

beats.scene: Captives in new clothes stand in a neat row in a yard
beats.summary: Freeman has them washed and dressed in new clothes so they will look healthy, and calls Solomon Platt, the name Burch gave him.

beats.scene: A dealer cracks a whip while captives dance and a man plays violin
beats.summary: Each day Freeman makes the captives stand, walk and dance to look lively, and Solomon is made to play the violin.

beats.scene: A buyer in a tall hat looks closely at a man's hands and teeth
beats.summary: Buyers come to inspect the captives: they feel their arms, look at their teeth and ask what each can do.

beats.scene: A boy is led out of a gate while his mother reaches for him
beats.summary: A buyer chooses the boy Randall, and Eliza, in terror, begs that she and her children be kept together.

beats.scene: A dealer raises his hand to silence a weeping woman in a crowded yard
beats.summary: Freeman answers Eliza's pleading with anger and threats; her sobbing goes on for days.

beats.scene: A mild-looking planter speaks with Freeman at a table, papers between them
beats.summary: William Ford, a Baptist preacher from the Red River country, comes to buy; he is moved by Eliza's grief, and buys Solomon and Eliza.

beats.scene: A girl clings to her mother's dress while a dealer pulls her away
beats.summary: Eliza leaves with Ford, but her daughter Emily is kept back by Freeman; Solomon never forgets the mother's cry.

beats.scene: A steamboat moves slowly up a river, a planter and two captives on deck
beats.summary: Ford takes Solomon and Eliza up the Mississippi and the Red River by steamboat, speaking kindly to Solomon on the way.

beats.scene: A plain wooden house among pine trees, a cabin and a sawmill behind it
beats.summary: After a last stage by wagon through the Pine Woods they reach Ford's home; Mrs Ford welcomes them, and Solomon spends his first night in a cabin.

beats.scene: A planter reads from a Bible under a tree to a gathered crowd
beats.summary: Ford is a Baptist minister, gentle and fair by the standards of the place, who reads the Bible aloud on Sundays to those he holds.

beats.scene: Men feed a long pine log into a water-powered sawmill
beats.summary: Solomon works at Ford's sawmill among the tall pines, using the skills he learned on the canals of New York.

beats.scene: Heavy wagons stuck in a sandy road beside a stack of planks
beats.summary: Ford has a large order of planks to deliver, but hauling them by wagon along the sandy road is slow and costly.

beats.scene: A man draws a raft plan in the sand while Ford watches
beats.summary: Solomon tells Ford that on the canals of New York he floated timber on rafts, and proposes floating the planks down a narrow creek.

beats.scene: A man steers a raft of logs down a narrow creek
beats.summary: Solomon builds the raft and takes it down the creek himself; it works, and Ford is pleased with his cleverness.

beats.scene: Ford shakes hands with Solomon in front of the mill while others look on
beats.summary: Ford praises Solomon in front of his neighbours; Solomon is treated well, yet nothing can make him forget that he is not free.

beats.scene: Wagons and workers set out along a sandy road at dawn
beats.summary: Ford takes up new business on Bayou Boeuf and moves there, taking Solomon with him.

beats.scene: Ford sits at a desk with papers, worried, a lamp beside him
beats.summary: Ford is in debt, and to pay what he owes he sells Solomon to a carpenter named John Tibeats, keeping a mortgage of four hundred dollars on him.

beats.scene: A hot-tempered man in a rough shirt shouts at Solomon in a workshop
beats.summary: Tibeats is a quick-tempered, petty man who finds fault with everything Solomon does, however well he works.

beats.scene: A young overseer on horseback looks across a half-built wall
beats.summary: They build a weaving house while Tibeats insults Solomon at every step; Chapin, Ford's fair-minded overseer, watches and says little.

beats.scene: Tibeats shouts at Solomon across a pile of boards and a box of nails
beats.summary: One morning, angry over the nails for the building, Tibeats tells Solomon that he will whip him.

beats.scene: Two men struggle by a half-built wall while a whip lies on the ground
beats.summary: When Tibeats tries to whip him, Solomon seizes the whip and turns it on his master.

beats.scene: Three men with a rope walk quickly across a field in the afternoon
beats.summary: Tibeats runs to a neighbouring plantation and comes back with two men and a rope.

beats.scene: Hands tie Solomon's wrists while a noose swings from a tree branch
beats.summary: The men tie his hands, put a noose round his neck and drag him to a tree.

beats.scene: A young overseer with pistols stands between three men and a tree
beats.summary: Chapin comes running with pistols and tells them that Solomon belongs to Ford, who holds a mortgage on him; he will not allow him to be hanged.

beats.scene: A man stands tied, a noose at his neck, in the sun
beats.summary: Tibeats and his friends leave, but Chapin does not cut the rope; Solomon is left standing in the sun, his hands tied and the noose still round his neck.

beats.scene: Faces watch from a cabin door, afraid to come forward
beats.summary: Through the long afternoon Solomon stands in pain while people watch from a distance, too afraid to help.

beats.scene: A gentle planter cuts the rope as a man sags in the afternoon sun
beats.summary: Ford returns in the afternoon and cuts the rope; Solomon has been hanging there for hours.

beats.scene: Ford sits beside Solomon in a lamplit room while his wife brings water
beats.summary: Ford listens to the whole story, says that Solomon was right to defend himself, and fears what Tibeats will do next.

beats.scene: A man grips a hatchet, then runs across a field toward the dark trees
beats.summary: Next morning Tibeats attacks him with a hatchet; Solomon seizes it from him and runs.

beats.scene: Hounds bay behind a man running towards a line of dark trees
beats.summary: Tibeats sets the hounds on his trail; Solomon runs for the swamp, where the water will hide his scent.

beats.scene: A man wades through a dark swamp, water to his knees
beats.summary: He wades for hours through black water among cypress trees, so that the dogs cannot follow his scent.

beats.scene: A man crouches under mossy cypress trees at night, stars through the branches
beats.summary: Night falls in the swamp; the noises, the mosquitoes and the cold keep him awake.

beats.scene: A water snake glides past a man standing in dark swamp water
beats.summary: By daylight he finds snakes in the water and alligators on the banks, and learns to move slowly.

beats.scene: A weary man comes out of woods towards a distant house at dawn
beats.summary: After a day and a night in the swamp he finds his way to open ground and walks towards Ford's house.

beats.scene: Ford stands at his door, giving bread to an exhausted man
beats.summary: Ford hears the whole story, gives him food and a bed, and promises that no one will harm him on the plantation.

beats.scene: Tibeats argues with Ford at a gate, hounds and men waiting behind him
beats.summary: Tibeats comes with men and dogs and demands Solomon; Ford refuses to give him up.

beats.scene: Ford hands a folded note to Solomon at a crossroads
beats.summary: To keep him out of Tibeats' reach, Ford sends Solomon to work for a time for Peter Tanner, his brother-in-law.

beats.scene: A strict planter watches workers hoe a field, a whip at his belt
beats.summary: Solomon works for some months on Tanner's farm, where the discipline is hard and he sees how much kinder Ford had been.

beats.scene: Two men shake hands over papers beside a waiting wagon
beats.summary: In the end Solomon is sold to Edwin Epps, a planter on Bayou Boeuf.

beats.scene: A wagon rolls along a muddy bayou road towards a large plantation
beats.summary: Solomon is taken to Epps's plantation on Bayou Boeuf, in the cotton country of Louisiana, where he will remain for about ten years.

beats.scene: A heavy man with a whip stands by rows of cotton at sunrise
beats.summary: Epps is a harsh planter who drinks heavily and is quick to whip; he believes that he may do what he likes with the people he holds.

beats.scene: Workers stand outside cabins at dawn, an old man among them
beats.summary: Solomon meets the others who work for Epps, among them old Uncle Abram, Aunt Phebe, Wiley and a young woman named Patsey.

beats.scene: Rows of white cotton under a hot sun and bent workers with long sacks
beats.summary: On his first day in the cotton field Solomon is slow, since he has never picked cotton; he learns that each person must bring in about two hundred pounds.

beats.scene: Workers line up at dusk with full sacks beside a barn and a scale
beats.summary: At night each person's cotton is weighed in the barn; those who fall short are whipped, and Solomon is warned that he will be too if he does not improve.

beats.scene: A young woman picks cotton with both hands, far ahead of the others
beats.summary: By watching Patsey, who picks much more than anyone else, Solomon slowly learns to pick enough to stay safe.

beats.scene: A bare wooden cabin with a plank bed and a small fire at night
beats.summary: At night the people sleep for a few hours on a plank in a cabin, after grinding their own corn for a meagre supper.

beats.scene: A man plays a violin by firelight in a bare cabin while others listen
beats.summary: In time Solomon gets a violin again and plays it in the evenings; the music does not end his pain, but it reminds him that he is still himself.

beats.scene: People wash clothes and mend shirts outside cabins on a Sunday
beats.summary: Sunday is the one day not spent in the cotton field; the people wash and mend their clothes and rest as best they can.

beats.scene: Epps staggers into the quarters at night with a bottle, shouting for music
beats.summary: When Epps has been drinking, he wakes everyone at night and orders them to dance while Solomon plays; those who stop are whipped.

beats.scene: Mules draw ploughs along the first spring furrows
beats.summary: The cotton year begins in spring, when the ground is ploughed and the seed is sown in long straight rows.

beats.scene: Workers hoe weeds between rows of young cotton in early summer heat
beats.summary: In early summer the people chop out weeds between the young plants with hoes, row after row, in the heat.

beats.scene: White cotton bolls burst open across a field in late summer
beats.summary: In late summer the cotton bolls open and the picking begins; from dawn to dusk everyone bends over the rows.

beats.scene: A woman picks with both hands and drops cotton into a long sack
beats.summary: Skilled pickers use both hands and never stop; the dry bolls cut the fingers, and the sack grows heavier through the day.

beats.scene: A wagon of cotton rolls to the gin house at dusk
beats.summary: Each night the cotton is weighed and stored; later it is ginned to remove the seeds and pressed into bales.

beats.scene: A steamboat loaded with cotton bales moves down a bayou
beats.summary: The bales go by steamboat to New Orleans and from there to mills in the North and in England; Solomon thinks of the shirts that the cotton will become.

beats.scene: Mounted men ride along a dark road at night carrying lanterns
beats.summary: No one may leave the plantation without a written pass from the master; patrols ride at night to stop and punish those without one.

beats.scene: Epps hands Solomon a whip in the cotton field while others watch
beats.summary: For a time Epps makes Solomon carry a whip in the field and drive the others; Solomon cracks it near them but dares not strike.

beats.scene: A man alone at dusk looks across a field, his lips pressed shut
beats.summary: Solomon never lets anyone know that he can read and write; he knows that such a man would be thought dangerous and might be sold farther away.

beats.scene: A man sits by a cabin door at dusk, looking up at the stars
beats.summary: Solomon decides to say little, work well and hide a secret hope; he is sure that some chance will come if he can only live to see it.

beats.scene: A young woman laughs among the cotton rows, a basket on her hip
beats.summary: Patsey, about twenty, is the best cotton picker on the plantation, cheerful and quick; her skill brings her more trouble than praise.

beats.scene: An angry woman watches from a porch as Patsey walks past
beats.summary: Epps's attention to Patsey makes his wife Mary jealous and spiteful, and Patsey suffers from both of them.

beats.scene: A heavy glass bottle shatters against a wall beside a young woman
beats.summary: Mary Epps's hatred grows so bitter that she once throws a heavy glass bottle at Patsey and often refuses her even a little soap.

beats.scene: A young woman walks along a dusty path at dusk towards a neighbour's gate
beats.summary: Refused soap by her mistress, Patsey walks to a neighbouring plantation to ask for a piece; Epps, back from town, finds her missing.

beats.scene: Epps stands over a young woman with a whip while others watch in silence
beats.summary: Epps does not believe that she went only for soap; in a rage he orders four stakes driven into the ground and Patsey tied to them.

beats.scene: A man holds a whip, unwilling, while another stands over him
beats.summary: Epps orders Solomon to whip Patsey; Solomon strikes lightly, then refuses to go on, and Epps takes the whip himself.

beats.scene: Women lift a limp young woman gently from the ground at dusk
beats.summary: When it is over the other women carry Patsey to her cabin, where she lies for days; Solomon and the others do what little they can.

beats.scene: A young woman sits silent at a cabin door, head bowed
beats.summary: After that day Patsey is no longer the girl she was: she stops laughing and singing and moves like someone in a dream.

beats.scene: A man bends to speak quietly with a young woman beside the bayou
beats.summary: In despair Patsey tells Solomon that she wishes she could die; he answers that while she lives there is still some hope.

beats.scene: Two people pick cotton side by side in the first light
beats.summary: Slowly Patsey returns to her work and the others look after her; Solomon never forgets what he saw, and it strengthens his wish to escape.

beats.scene: Workers swing long knives through tall green sugar cane
beats.summary: In autumn, when the cotton is picked, Epps hires out his people to other planters, and Solomon becomes skilled at cutting sugar cane.

beats.scene: Rows of cut cane lie in a field while a mule cart waits
beats.summary: The cane is cut at the base, stripped of its leaves and loaded into carts for the sugar mill, the cutters working in a long line.

beats.scene: Steam rises from huge kettles in a sugar-house at night
beats.summary: At the sugar-house the cane is crushed and the juice boiled down; in the grinding season the work goes on day and night.

beats.scene: Workers from several plantations talk together at the edge of a cane field
beats.summary: In the cane fields Solomon meets people from many plantations and hears how so many of them were sold away from their homes in the older states.

beats.scene: People in their best clothes gather around a long table outdoors
beats.summary: At Christmas the people are given about three days free; they put on their best clothes and there is a supper and a dance.

beats.scene: A man plays the violin in a bright ballroom among dancers
beats.summary: At Christmas Solomon is often hired to play the violin at balls given by white planters; he earns a few dollars and sees many houses.

beats.scene: A man walks a bayou road holding a paper pass
beats.summary: Going out with passes, Solomon learns the roads, bayous and plantations of the district, and builds a map of it in his mind.

beats.scene: A man hides a few coins in a cloth beneath a plank
beats.summary: Solomon hides the few dollars he earns, knowing that money might one day buy paper, ink or a letter's journey.

beats.scene: A line of hounds on leashes waits at the edge of a swamp
beats.summary: Runaways are hunted with dogs, and the free states lie more than a thousand miles away; Solomon sees that to run alone would mean capture or death.

beats.scene: A man looks north at dusk over a field of cotton stubble
beats.summary: Solomon resolves to wait for the right chance and to find, if he can, one person he can trust with his secret.

beats.scene: Cotton rows under changing seasons: green, white, bare, then green again
beats.summary: Year follows year in the same round of ploughing, hoeing, picking and cane cutting; Solomon counts the seasons since the spring of 1841.

beats.scene: A man lies awake in a dark cabin, listening to the frogs outside
beats.summary: At night he remembers the streets and church bells of Saratoga and imagines Anne in the kitchen with the children round her.

beats.scene: A woman waits at a kitchen window in the evening, watching the road
beats.summary: He wonders what Anne believes has become of him, and fears that she may think him dead.

beats.scene: Three children stand in a row, each a little taller than the last
beats.summary: He counts the ages of Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo and knows that they must be grown; he fears that they may have forgotten him.

beats.scene: A sick man lies on a plank while a master stands at the door
beats.summary: In the summer heat fever sweeps the quarters; Epps thinks only of the work that is lost, and the sick are sent back to the field as soon as they can stand.

beats.scene: A man staggers across a yard with a bottle while a woman shouts
beats.summary: Epps drinks more heavily as the years pass, and the quarrels between him and his wife fill the big house; the people in the quarters pay for them.

beats.scene: Dark clouds and heavy rain fall on a flooded cotton field
beats.summary: In a bad year the crop is ruined by rain or insects; Epps blames the workers, and the people are hired out to make up his loss.

beats.scene: People sit around a small fire at night while one man talks
beats.summary: Sometimes, at night, the others ask Solomon about the North, and he tells them of snow, railroads and schools where black children learn to read.

beats.scene: A newspaper lies folded on a porch rail beside a pair of boots
beats.summary: News reaches the plantation only in scraps: far away the argument over slavery grows hotter, and in 1850 Congress passes a harsher Fugitive Slave Act.

beats.scene: A man stands alone in a field, looking at the horizon
beats.summary: After eleven years Solomon is still alive and still remembers that his name is Solomon Northup; he has not given up.

beats.scene: A man in a dark cabin stares at a corner, thinking of letters
beats.summary: Solomon longs to write to his friends in New York, but he has no paper, no ink and no pen, and to be caught would be dangerous.

beats.scene: A man slips a folded sheet of paper into his shirt
beats.summary: At last he manages to take a single sheet of paper when no one is looking.

beats.scene: A small pot of dark liquid simmers over a tiny fire in a cabin
beats.summary: He makes ink by boiling the bark of a maple tree in a little water.

beats.scene: A man trims a long feather with a small knife by firelight
beats.summary: He cuts a pen from a duck's feather with his small knife.

beats.scene: A man writes slowly by firelight on a single sheet of paper
beats.summary: Working at night by the glow of the fire, he writes a letter that tells his friends where he is and begs for help, then hides it.

beats.scene: A poor labourer leans on a fence and speaks quietly to Solomon
beats.summary: A poor white labourer named Armsby is working for Epps; Solomon thinks he may be willing to post the letter, and Armsby agrees, for a price.

beats.scene: Epps confronts Solomon in the yard, one finger raised
beats.summary: Armsby betrays Solomon to Epps, who demands to know what he has been doing.

beats.scene: Epps frowns at a man who is talking quickly and calmly in the yard
beats.summary: Solomon says that Armsby is lying, and that the man was only trying to trick him out of his money; Epps believes him rather than a stranger.

beats.scene: A folded letter curls and blackens in a small fire
beats.summary: That night Solomon burns the letter, with the pen and the ink, so that nothing can be found.

beats.scene: A man lies awake on his plank in the dark, staring at nothing
beats.summary: Solomon lies awake and knows how close he came to being sold farther away or killed; he decides never to trust anyone until he is certain.

beats.scene: Carpenters raise the timber frame of a large new house
beats.summary: In 1852 Epps decides to build a new house and hires carpenters, among them a man named Samuel Bass, who comes from Canada.

beats.scene: A carpenter with a toolbox walks up a dusty road to a plantation house
beats.summary: Bass has travelled in many places and lived by his trade; he is plain-spoken and he is not afraid to say what he thinks.

beats.scene: Bass talks with the workers at midday while Solomon passes with a pail
beats.summary: Solomon notices that Bass speaks to the people on the plantation as equals, without contempt or fear.

beats.scene: Two men argue beside a half-built wall while a third listens
beats.summary: Bass argues with Epps that slavery is wrong; Epps laughs at him, but Bass speaks plainly and Solomon, listening, is deeply moved.

beats.scene: Bass raises one hand to make a point while Epps shakes his head
beats.summary: Bass says that a law may allow a wrong without making it right, and that the day will come when it is changed.

beats.scene: Epps leans back in a porch chair, laughing, a glass in hand
beats.summary: Epps thinks Bass odd but cannot deny that he is a fine carpenter, and he lets him talk.

beats.scene: Bass puts down his hammer and speaks quietly to Solomon
beats.summary: One evening Bass asks Solomon some quiet questions: how long he has lived on the plantation, and whether he is content to be a slave; Solomon answers with great care.

beats.scene: A man stands in the doorway at night, looking towards the half-built house
beats.summary: Solomon weighs the risk for days: if he is wrong, he may be killed; but this is the first white man in eleven years who has spoken openly against slavery.

beats.scene: A carpenter sits on a log in the evening, telling a story
beats.summary: Bass tells of his wanderings: he was born in Canada, has lived in many states, has never owned a person and never will.

beats.scene: A man looks at the unfinished house against a red sky at dusk
beats.summary: Solomon decides to take the risk and speak to Bass; he waits only for a quiet moment when no one else is near.

beats.scene: Two men sit on a plank in the dark outside a cabin
beats.summary: One quiet evening, with no one near, Solomon asks Bass whether he can keep a secret; Bass says that he can.

beats.scene: A man speaks in a low voice, hands open on his knees
beats.summary: Solomon tells Bass his real name and the whole story: Saratoga, Anne and the children, Brown and Hamilton, Washington, Burch and the years since.

beats.scene: A carpenter sits with his face in his hands as a lamp burns low
beats.summary: Bass is deeply shaken by the story; he tells Solomon that he believes every word and that he will do all he can.

beats.scene: Bass looks over his shoulder towards the big house in the dusk
beats.summary: Bass warns that if his plan were discovered in that place, his own life would be in danger; but he has made up his mind.

beats.scene: A man counts names on his fingers while another listens
beats.summary: Bass asks for the names of friends who would help, and Solomon gives him two Saratoga merchants, Parker and Perry, who have known him for years.

beats.scene: Two men talk quietly beneath a tree while workers pass at a distance
beats.summary: They agree to be careful: they will never speak of it where they can be overheard, and in public Bass will treat Solomon as any other worker.

beats.scene: A man writes at a table by candlelight and seals a letter
beats.summary: That night Bass writes to Parker and Perry in Saratoga, telling them where Solomon is and begging them to send help and proof of his freedom.

beats.scene: A man drops a letter into a box at a small post office
beats.summary: Bass posts the letter in Marksville; it will take weeks to reach New York, and Solomon can only wait.

beats.scene: A man lies awake in the dark and smiles
beats.summary: After eleven years Solomon at last has a friend who knows the truth; he sleeps little that night, because hope is almost as hard to bear as despair.

beats.scene: Two men shake hands in the lamplight
beats.summary: Bass promises that if no answer has come by Christmas, he will travel north himself in the spring to find Solomon's friends.

beats.scene: A carpenter walks away down a road with his toolbox over his shoulder
beats.summary: The new house is finished, and Bass leaves for Marksville, promising to return; Solomon watches him go.

beats.scene: A man cuts notches into a wooden post, counting the days
beats.summary: Picking begins again, and Solomon counts the weeks, for a letter takes a long time to reach New York and an answer a long time to return.

beats.scene: Two merchants read a letter together in a shop, one pointing at a line
beats.summary: In Saratoga the letter reaches Parker and Perry, who are astonished to learn that Solomon is alive; they take it to his wife.

beats.scene: A woman holds a letter to her chest as her children gather round
beats.summary: Anne and the children read that Solomon is alive; after eleven years of silence, they weep for joy and fear.

beats.scene: A lawyer reads a letter at his desk in a small town
beats.summary: Anne takes the letter to Henry B Northup, a lawyer at Sandy Hill, whose family once owned Solomon's father; he agrees at once to help.

beats.scene: A lawyer turns the pages of a thick law book by lamplight
beats.summary: Henry finds that a New York law of 1840 lets the governor send an agent to recover a free citizen who has been kidnapped and sold into slavery.

beats.scene: Neighbours sign a paper at a table while a lawyer holds out a pen
beats.summary: Henry collects sworn statements from many Saratoga neighbours that Solomon was born free and had lived there for years.

beats.scene: A lawyer hands a bundle of papers to a governor in a grand office
beats.summary: Henry takes the statements to Albany, where Governor Washington Hunt gives him official authority to bring Solomon home; winter is setting in.

beats.scene: A man plays the violin by firelight on Christmas night, looking at the road
beats.summary: In Louisiana Christmas comes with its three free days, but Bass does not appear; Solomon plays the violin and watches the road.

beats.scene: A man picks cotton in the cold dawn with a heavy heart
beats.summary: Christmas passes with no word; Solomon returns to the cotton field in the new year, almost without hope, wondering whether Bass has forgotten him.

beats.scene: A lawyer boards a train in the snow with a leather bag
beats.summary: Henry sets out from the north with his papers; his first stop is Washington, where he asks for help from men in authority.

beats.scene: A steamboat moves slowly down the wide Mississippi with a man at the rail
beats.summary: From Washington he goes on by rail and steamboat down the Mississippi, a long journey in winter.

beats.scene: A man studies a map spread out on a hotel table
beats.summary: At New Orleans Henry asks the way to Bayou Boeuf and learns that he must first go to Marksville, the seat of the parish, and put his case to the law there.

beats.scene: A small steamer carries passengers up a brown river between flat green banks
beats.summary: He goes on by steamer up the Red River, through cypress swamps and cotton country, towards Marksville.

beats.scene: A small southern courthouse town, with a square and a few shops
beats.summary: At Marksville Henry meets a lawyer named John P Waddill, who agrees to help him bring Solomon's case before the court.

beats.scene: A lawyer and a visitor sit across a desk, the visitor leaning forward
beats.summary: Waddill explains that the law of Louisiana protects owners, so Henry must prove Solomon is free and act through the court, not by force.

beats.scene: A lawyer writes a legal petition by candlelight, his pen scratching
beats.summary: Waddill draws up a petition asking the court to order the sheriff to take Solomon from Epps and bring him before the judge; the judge signs it.

beats.scene: A sheriff and a lawyer climb into a carriage in the early morning
beats.summary: The sheriff and Henry set out for Bayou Boeuf with the court's order; Henry plans to find Solomon quietly in the field rather than go to the house.

beats.scene: A carriage rolls along a muddy bayou road between cotton fields
beats.summary: Following directions from people they meet on the road, they come at last to the edge of Epps's land and see a gang of workers in a cotton field.

beats.scene: A carriage stops on a dusty road and two men step down
beats.summary: They leave the carriage at the roadside and walk towards the field; it is the third of January 1853.

beats.scene: A man picks cotton in a long line while two strangers cross the field
beats.summary: Two strangers walk across the cotton field towards the workers; Solomon goes on picking, and does not look up.

beats.scene: A man in a cotton field looks up as another calls his name
beats.summary: One of them asks him his name; Solomon says Platt, the name he has used for twelve years, and then the stranger asks if he knows him.

beats.scene: Two men clasp hands in a cotton field as the workers stand frozen
beats.summary: Solomon recognises Henry B Northup, who calls him by his real name, Solomon Northup; for a moment he cannot speak, and then he weeps.

beats.scene: A heavy man with a whip strides across a field towards two strangers
beats.summary: Epps hurries up, red with anger, but the sheriff shows the court's order and tells him that Platt is a free man named Solomon Northup.

beats.scene: Epps shouts and points while a calm sheriff holds up a paper
beats.summary: Epps rages and swears that he bought Platt honestly and will not give him up, but the law is plain and he can do nothing to stop it.

beats.scene: A man hurries between cabins gathering a few things into a small bundle
beats.summary: Solomon is told that he may go at once; he has almost nothing to take, only a bundle of rags and the violin that he has played for many years.

beats.scene: A young woman runs from the cabins and clasps a man's arm, weeping
beats.summary: Patsey runs after him weeping and clings to him; Epps orders her back, and Solomon, in grief, can do nothing to help her.

beats.scene: People stand together in front of the cabins, watching a carriage
beats.summary: The others stand in a group and watch; some call out blessings, but they cannot follow; Solomon never sees any of them again.

beats.scene: A furious planter stands at a gate as a carriage rolls away
beats.summary: Epps stands at the gate, shouting angrily, as the carriage pulls away; Solomon looks back until the plantation is out of sight.

beats.scene: A small-town courtroom with a judge and men at a table
beats.summary: At Marksville the judge hears the proof and Solomon is declared free; the legal papers are completed.

beats.scene: A steamboat sails down a brown river, a man at the rail
beats.summary: Solomon and Henry go down the Red River and the Mississippi to New Orleans; for the first time in twelve years he travels as a free passenger.

beats.scene: A man stands on a busy wharf, looking at the ships
beats.summary: At New Orleans Solomon walks the streets where he had been sold, and sees the wharf where the Orleans landed him.

beats.scene: A lawyer and a dealer face each other across a table
beats.summary: In Washington Henry and Solomon find James Burch, who is arrested for kidnapping.

beats.scene: Burch sits among lawyers in a courtroom while a young man waits
beats.summary: In court Burch says that he bought Solomon in good faith; the court will not accept a Black man's word against a white man's, and the case against Burch collapses.

beats.scene: A train runs through snowy hills towards a small northern town
beats.summary: From Washington they go north by train through the winter landscape; Solomon, who has not been home for twelve years, can think of nothing else.

beats.scene: A family embraces on a snowy porch, a young woman holding a baby
beats.summary: In January 1853 Solomon returns to his family in the Sandy Hill and Glens Falls country, where Anne and the children are waiting; they have grown up, and a grandson bears his name.

beats.scene: A man stands bareheaded in a snowy yard beside a wooden fence
beats.summary: Solomon learns what has happened in his absence: his mother has died, and his children have grown up; everyone had thought that he was dead.

beats.scene: A man writes at a table with a second man listening and taking notes
beats.summary: With the help of a local writer, David Wilson, Solomon puts his story into a book, which he dedicates to Harriet Beecher Stowe.

beats.scene: People crowd around a bookseller's table in a northern city in 1853
beats.summary: The book is published in 1853 and widely read; it sells many thousands of copies, and Solomon speaks to meetings; none of the men who stole him is ever punished.

beats.scene: A young reader sits quietly beside a window holding an open old book
beats.summary: Slavery in the United States ended only in 1865; today the book is read around the world as one of the clearest first-hand accounts of slavery and asks us to value freedom for everyone.

A1A2: In 1853, Solomon Northup told the true story of his stolen life.
Solomon was born free in New York in 1808, in the month of July.
Mintus belonged to the Northup family, and his master freed him in his will.
Mintus taught his son to read, to write, and to farm the land.
Solomon loved music, and he played the violin for dances in the village.
As a young man, he worked on boats and rafts on the canal.
On Christmas Day 1829, Solomon married a kind young woman, Anne Hampton.
Solomon and Anne had three young children, and he loved them dearly.
In 1834, the family moved to Saratoga Springs, a busy town with hotels.
Solomon was thirty-two, and he had a home, work and good friends.
One day in March, two well-dressed men stopped and spoke to Solomon.
They said a circus needed a violin player, and the pay was good.
Solomon wanted to ask Anne, but she was away with the children.
He packed a small bag of clothes, and then they left at once.
From Albany, a boat took them down the river to New York City.
Brown said free papers would be useful, so Solomon went and got them.
They went south by boat and train, and Solomon watched the new land.
They arrived in Washington, where the city was sad and the flags were low.
Solomon walked around the city and saw the great Capitol building.
Soldiers and bands walked slowly through the streets for the dead President.
After supper, Solomon felt very ill and went to his room.
Solomon woke on a cold stone floor, in a dark room.
He called for Brown and Hamilton, but nobody came to the door.
A man named Burch came in and called him a runaway slave.
Burch beat him hard until Solomon said no more about freedom.
Burch said that if Solomon told anyone he was free, he would die.
In the yard, he could see the dome of the Capitol.
Many people were held there, and all feared the journey south.
Eliza wept all day, and her two children stayed close beside her.
Each night Solomon thought of home, but he could send no message.
One night, Burch took them out of the pen in chains.
A steamboat took them down the river, and nobody helped them.
A train took them on to Richmond, and passengers did not look.
In Richmond, they were put in another pen to wait.
Solomon met Robert and Arthur, who also said they were free men.
They were put on a ship called the Orleans, which sailed south.
Solomon, Robert and Arthur secretly planned to take over the ship.
Then a bad sickness began on the ship, and Robert became ill.
Robert died, and the plan to take the ship was over.
At last the ship came up the great river to New Orleans.
They walked from the ship to the pen of a dealer named Freeman.
Freeman called him Platt, and Solomon was afraid to say no.
Every day, Freeman made them dance, and Solomon played the violin.
Buyers came to look at them, and they asked many questions.
A man bought the boy Randall, and his mother cried out.
Freeman was angry, but Eliza could not stop crying.
A kind man named William Ford came and bought Solomon and Eliza.
Emily had to stay behind, and her mother cried out in pain.
Ford took them up the river by steamboat, and he spoke kindly to Solomon.
At Ford's house, Solomon was given food and a place to sleep.
William Ford was a preacher, and on Sundays he read the Bible aloud.
Solomon worked at Ford's mill, where tall pine trees were cut into boards.
Ford had to carry many boards a long way, and it was slow.
Solomon said planks could float on a raft down the creek.
Solomon built a raft and floated the boards down the creek.
Ford praised Solomon, but Solomon still wanted to be free.
Later, Ford moved to a new place called Bayou Boeuf.
Ford owed money, so he had to sell Solomon to a man named Tibeats.
Tibeats was angry and mean, and he shouted at Solomon every day.
Chapin, Ford's overseer, watched them work and said little.
One morning, Tibeats shouted about the nails and said he would whip Solomon.
Solomon took the whip from Tibeats and used it on him.
Tibeats ran away, and he came back with two men and a rope.
The men tied his hands and put a rope round his neck.
Chapin came with two pistols and told the men to stop.
Tibeats left, but Solomon was still tied and standing in the sun.
Many people saw him there, but they were afraid to help.
At last Ford came home and cut the rope with his own knife.
Ford listened to the whole story and said Solomon was right.
The next morning, Tibeats tried to hurt Solomon, but Solomon ran away.
Dogs began to follow him, so Solomon ran toward the swamp.
Solomon waded for hours through the cold, dark swamp water.
Night came, and Solomon could not sleep in the swamp.
In the morning, he saw many snakes in the dark water.
At last he left the swamp and walked toward Ford's house.
Ford fed him and gave him a bed, and Solomon slept well.
Tibeats came and demanded Solomon, but Ford said no.
To keep Solomon safe, Ford sent him to work for Peter Tanner.
Tanner was a hard man, and Solomon missed Ford very much.
In the end, Solomon was sold to a planter named Edwin Epps.
Solomon was taken to Epps's plantation, where he would stay many years.
Epps was a hard man who drank a lot and often used his whip.
Solomon met the other workers, old and young, and they were kind to him.
On his first day, Solomon was slow, because he had never picked cotton.
At night, the cotton was weighed, and those with too little were whipped.
Patsey picked more cotton than anyone, and Solomon learned from her.
At night, they slept for a few hours on a hard plank.
In time, Solomon found a violin again, and he played it in the evenings.
On Sunday, there was no cotton to pick, and people washed their clothes.
When Epps was drunk, he woke them at night to dance.
In spring, the people worked the fields and planted cotton seed.
In summer, they worked all day in the heat, taking weeds from the rows.
In late summer, the cotton opened, and everyone began to pick.
Good workers used both hands, and the dry plants cut their fingers.
At night the cotton was weighed, and later it was pressed into bales.
The cotton went by boat to New Orleans, and then to far places.
No one could leave Epps's land without a paper from the master.
Epps made Solomon carry a whip and watch the other workers.
Solomon never told anyone that he could read and write.
Solomon decided to work hard, say little, and keep hoping.
Patsey was young and cheerful, and she picked more cotton than anyone.
Epps's wife was jealous of Patsey and treated her cruelly.
Mary Epps once threw a heavy glass bottle at Patsey.
Patsey needed soap, so she walked to a neighbour's house to ask for some.
Epps did not believe her, and he was very angry.
Epps told Solomon to whip her, but Solomon would not hurt her.
The women carried Patsey to her cabin, and she lay there for days.
After that day, Patsey no longer laughed or sang.
Patsey told Solomon she wished to die, but he told her to hope.
Patsey went back to work, and Solomon never forgot that day.
In autumn, Solomon cut tall sugar cane with a long, heavy knife.
They cut the cane, took off the leaves, and loaded it on carts.
At the sugar mill, they crushed the cane and boiled the sweet juice.
In the cane fields, Solomon met people from many different farms.
At Christmas, they had a few days free, with a supper and dancing.
Many people wanted Solomon to play the violin at their parties.
With a pass, Solomon learned the roads and rivers of the district.
Solomon hid the small amount of money that he earned.
Runaways were hunted with dogs, and the free states were far away.
Solomon decided to wait, and to look for one person he could trust.
The years went by in the same way: planting, picking, and cutting cane.
At night, Solomon remembered the streets of his home town.
He wondered what Anne thought, and if she believed he was dead.
Solomon counted how old his children were now, and he wondered about them.
In summer, many people had fever, but they still had to work.
Epps drank more each year, and he and his wife often shouted.
In a bad year, the rain or insects spoiled the cotton.
Sometimes, the others asked Solomon about the free North.
News came slowly, and Solomon heard little about the outside world.
Solomon was still alive, and he still knew his own name.
Solomon wanted to write to his friends, but he had no paper or pen.
At last, he took one sheet of paper when nobody was looking.
He boiled some tree bark in water to make dark ink.
He made a pen from a duck's feather and cut it with a knife.
At night, by the fire, Solomon wrote a letter to his friends.
A poor white worker named Armsby said he would post the letter.
But Armsby told Epps about the letter, and Epps was angry.
Solomon said that Armsby was lying, and Epps believed him.
That night, Solomon burned the letter, and he felt very sad.
Solomon lay awake and decided not to trust any more people.
In 1852, Epps began to build a new house, and he hired carpenters.
Bass had lived in many places, and he said what he thought.
Bass spoke to the black workers as equals, without contempt.
Bass told Epps that slavery was wrong, and Epps laughed.
Bass said that a law can allow a wrong, but it is still wrong.
Epps thought Bass was odd, but he needed a good carpenter.
One day, Bass asked Solomon how long he had lived there.
Solomon thought about the risk, because he might be killed.
Bass said that he was born in Canada, and had never owned a slave.
Solomon decided to speak to Bass, and he waited for a quiet moment.
One quiet evening, Solomon asked Bass if he could keep a secret.
Solomon told Bass his real name, and the true story of his life.
Bass was shocked, and he said that he would help Solomon.
Bass said that helping Solomon would be dangerous for him too.
Bass asked for names, and Solomon gave him the names of two friends.
They agreed to be careful, and never to talk where others could hear.
That night, Bass wrote a letter to Solomon's friends in Saratoga.
Bass posted the letter, and Solomon had to wait for an answer.
That night, Solomon could not sleep, because he felt a new hope.
Bass promised to go north himself in the spring, if nobody answered.
The house was finished, and Bass left, but he promised to return.
Solomon counted the weeks while he picked cotton in the hot sun.
In Saratoga, Parker and Perry read the letter and were amazed.
Anne read the letter, and she cried with joy and with fear.
They took the letter to a lawyer named Henry Northup, who agreed to help.
A New York law helped to bring home free people who were taken.
Many neighbours signed a paper that said Solomon was a free man.
In Albany, the governor gave Henry papers that gave him the power to help.
At Christmas, Solomon played the violin and watched the road for Bass.
Christmas passed with no news, and Solomon went back to the cotton.
Henry left on a train, and he went first to Washington.
Henry travelled on by train and by steamboat down the great river.
In New Orleans, Henry learned he must first go to a town called Marksville.
Henry went up the Red River by boat, toward Marksville.
In Marksville, Henry met a lawyer who agreed to help him.
The lawyer said the law protected owners, so they must go to a judge.
The lawyer wrote a legal paper, and a judge signed it.
The sheriff and Henry left in a carriage for Epps's plantation.
They followed the road, and they asked people the way to Epps's farm.
The carriage stopped, and Henry and the sheriff got out and walked.
Two strangers walked across the field, but Solomon kept on picking.
One stranger asked his name, and Solomon said it was Platt.
Solomon knew the man, and he began to cry.
Epps hurried out, but the sheriff showed him the court's order.
Epps was furious, but there was nothing he could do.
Solomon was free to go, and he took only a few things.
Patsey ran to him and held him, and she cried and cried.
The others stood and watched, and they called out goodbye.
The carriage left, and Solomon looked back until he could not see the farm.
In Marksville, a judge said that Solomon was free.
Solomon and Henry went down the river by steamboat, and Solomon was free.
In New Orleans, Solomon saw the wharf where he had arrived in chains.
In Washington, Henry and Solomon found Burch, and he was arrested.
In court, Burch said that he had bought Solomon honestly, and he went free.
Solomon and Henry went north by train, and he thought only of home.
Anne and the children were waiting, and they held him for a long time.
Solomon learned that his mother had died, and that his children had grown up.
With David Wilson's help, Solomon wrote the story of his life in a book.
The book sold very well, and Solomon spoke to many people.
Today, people all over the world still read his true story.
B1B2: In 1853, a book appeared in New York with the title Twelve Years a Slave. Its author, Solomon Northup, was a free man who had been stolen from his family and sold into slavery.
Solomon was born in July 1808 in Minerva, a small town in New York State. His father, Mintus, had once been a slave, but he was set free when his master died.
Mintus had been the slave of a family named Northup in the north of New York State. When the old master died, his will gave Mintus his freedom, and Mintus kept the family name.
Mintus taught his son to read and write, which was unusual in those days. Solomon also learned to farm, and he worked beside his father in the fields.
As a boy Solomon fell in love with the violin and practised until he could play any tune he heard. Before long, neighbours were asking him to play at weddings and village dances.
As a young man he worked on the Champlain Canal, steering rafts of timber to market. One trip even took him north into Canada, where he saw cities that were new and wonderful to him.
In 1829 Solomon’s father died, and on Christmas Day that same year Solomon married Anne Hampton. They began married life with little money, but with great hope and plenty of work.
The young family lived and farmed near Fort Edward, and Anne earned a good name as a cook. Three children were born to them over the years: Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo.

In 1834 the family moved to Saratoga Springs, a busy town where rich visitors came to drink the spring water. Solomon found work at the big hotels and on building jobs, and Anne cooked in some of the busy hotel kitchens.
By the spring of 1841 Solomon was thirty-two years old, with a home, steady work and many friends. He had no way of knowing that his free life was about to end.
One day in March 1841, two well-dressed strangers stopped Solomon in the street. They called themselves Brown and Hamilton, and they spoke warmly about his famous skill with the violin.
They said that their circus needed a musician, and they offered a dollar a day and three dollars for each show. All Solomon had to do was travel with them to Washington, where the circus was waiting.
Solomon wanted to ask Anne’s opinion, but she and the children were away from home for the spring. In the end the good pay and the promise of a short trip won him over.
Solomon packed a small bag of clothes, expecting to be away for only a few weeks. The three men then set off by carriage for Albany, and Solomon waved goodbye to the street he knew so well.
From Albany a steamboat carried them down the Hudson River to New York City. Solomon watched the crowded docks and the great ships, and the noise of the city never seemed to stop.

Brown and Hamilton said it would be wise to carry papers proving that he was free, since they would travel through slave states. At the Custom House an official wrote out a certificate of freedom, and Solomon put it safely in his pocket.

The three men crossed the river and travelled south by train through Philadelphia and Baltimore. Solomon enjoyed every mile, for the journey was like a holiday and Brown and Hamilton were cheerful company.
They reached Washington while the city was in mourning for President Harrison, who had died only days before. Brown and Hamilton took rooms in a hotel and paid Solomon some of his wages in advance.

While they waited for the circus, Solomon walked through the wide streets and stared at the white Capitol, where the nation's laws were made. In that year slavery was still lawful in the capital, and people were bought and sold within sight of the Capitol.
On 10 April 1841 the funeral of President Harrison filled the streets of Washington. Solomon stood among the crowd and watched the soldiers, the bands and the black funeral carriage pass slowly by.
After supper and some wine, Solomon began to feel dizzy and ill, and he went to bed. He remembered pain, strange faces and voices, and then nothing at all.
When Solomon woke, he was lying on a cold stone floor in a dark room. His hands and feet were in chains, and his money and his free papers were gone.

When Solomon finally understood what had happened, Brown and Hamilton were nowhere to be found. He later came to believe that they had planned it all from the start and had sold him to a slave dealer.

At last a slave dealer named James Burch came in and told Solomon that he was a runaway from Georgia named Platt. Solomon answered that he was a free man from New York and that he had never been anyone's slave.
Because Solomon would not stop saying that he was free, Burch beat him with a wooden paddle until it broke. Then he took a whip, and the beating went on until Solomon was too weak to speak.
Burch warned him that he would be killed if he ever told anyone again that he was free. Solomon lay in pain and understood that the truth had become the most dangerous thing he could say.
During the day the captives were let out into a small yard with high walls. Over the top of the wall Solomon could see the white dome of the Capitol.
Many of the people in the pen were waiting to be sent south and sold. They spoke quietly of the homes and families they had left behind.

Solomon met a woman named Eliza, who was held in the pen with her two children, Emily and Randall. She told him that she had once been promised her freedom, but now she was to be sold, and she could not stop weeping.
Each night Solomon lay awake and thought of Anne and the children, wondering what they believed had become of him. He had no pen, no paper and no one he could trust to carry a message.
One night Burch woke the captives and had them taken out in chains. They were driven through the dark streets to the river, and Solomon looked back at the lamps of the Capitol.
A steamboat carried the captives down the Potomac River through the night. The other passengers walked about the deck, and none of them stopped to ask why the chained men and women were there.
From the river a train carried them on towards Richmond in Virginia. Once again the travellers around them took no notice, and Burch kept close watch over his captives.
In Richmond they were locked in another slave pen, like the one in Washington. The city was one of the busiest places for the slave trade in the whole country.
In the pen Solomon met two men named Robert and Arthur, who said that they, too, had once been free. They spoke in whispers at night, and it comforted Solomon to find that he was not alone.
From Richmond the captives were taken aboard a ship called the Orleans, which was bound for New Orleans. Below deck they slept in chains, and the hold was crowded and hot.

At sea Solomon, Robert and Arthur began to plan in whispers how they might take control of the ship. If they could seize it from the captain and the crew, they thought, they could sail it north to freedom.
Before the plan could be tried, smallpox broke out among the captives. Robert fell ill first, and Solomon was taken ill soon afterwards.
Robert did not recover, and the sailors dropped his body into the sea. Solomon slowly got better, but without Robert the plan to seize the ship was finished.
At last the ship turned into the mouth of the Mississippi and sailed up the wide brown river. New Orleans, where it landed, was one of the biggest slave markets in the country.
The captives were marched from the wharf past great piles of cotton bales to a slave pen in the city. It belonged to a dealer named Theophilus Freeman, who looked them over like goods.
Freeman had the captives washed and dressed in new clothes so that they would look strong and healthy. He called Solomon by the name Platt, and Solomon was too afraid to correct him.

Every day Freeman made the captives dance and move briskly, so that buyers would think they were strong and cheerful. Solomon was told to play the violin for the dancing, and he obeyed with a heavy heart.
Buyers came every day to look at the captives. They felt their arms, looked at their teeth, made them walk, and asked each one what work he could do.
One day a buyer chose the boy Randall and took him away from his mother. Eliza fell on her knees and begged to be kept with her children.
Freeman answered her pleading with anger, and he told her to stop her noise or be punished. Eliza did not stop, for her grief was greater than her fear.
A planter named William Ford, a preacher from the Red River country, came to the pen to buy people for his farm. He was moved by Eliza's grief, and he agreed to buy both her and Solomon.
Eliza was taken away with Ford, but her daughter Emily was kept behind by Freeman. Solomon never forgot the cry that Eliza gave as she was pulled away.
Ford took his two new workers up the Mississippi and then up the Red River by steamboat. On the way he spoke kindly to Solomon, which was not at all what Solomon had expected.
After a last long ride by wagon through the tall Pine Woods, they reached Ford's house, where his wife welcomed them kindly. Solomon was given supper and a place to sleep in a cabin near the sawmill.
William Ford was a Baptist minister who preached on Sundays and read the Bible aloud to the people he held. By the standards of that country he was gentle and fair, and Solomon never forgot it.
Solomon was put to work at Ford's sawmill, where the tall pines were cut into boards. His years on the canals had taught him a good deal about timber, and he worked quickly and carefully.
Ford had agreed to deliver a large order of planks to a distant builder. Carrying them by wagon over the deep, sandy road was slow and expensive, and he worried about the cost.

Solomon told Ford that, in New York, he had floated timber on rafts along the canal. He suggested that the planks could be tied together and floated down the narrow creek instead of being carried by wagon.
Solomon built the raft himself and steered it down the winding creek. The plan worked well, and the planks arrived faster and more cheaply than they would have by road.
Ford praised Solomon in front of his neighbours and told them that Platt was a clever fellow. Solomon was treated well, but kindness could not make him forget that he was not free.
After a time Ford decided to start a new business on Bayou Boeuf, a slow stream in a rich farming country. He moved his household there and took Solomon with him.
Ford owed money, and to pay his debt he had to sell Solomon to a carpenter named John Tibeats. He kept a mortgage of four hundred dollars on Solomon, which meant that he still had a claim on him.
Tibeats was a small, hot-tempered man who could not bear to be told that he was wrong. He found fault with everything Solomon did, however well he did it.
Solomon and Tibeats began to build a weaving house, with Tibeats insulting him at every step. A fair-minded young overseer named Chapin, who worked for Ford, watched them and said little.
One morning Tibeats flew into a rage over a box of nails, although Solomon had done exactly as he was told. He picked up a whip and said that he would teach Solomon a lesson.
When Tibeats tried to whip him, Solomon seized the whip and the two men struggled by the half-built wall. In the end Solomon turned the whip on his master, and Tibeats screamed for help.
Tibeats ran off to a nearby plantation, and in a short time he returned with two other men and a rope. They had come to punish Solomon in the cruellest way they could.
The three men tied Solomon's hands behind him and put a noose around his neck. They dragged him to a tree and began to throw the rope over a branch.
Just then Chapin, the overseer, came running with a pistol in each hand. He told the men that Solomon was Ford's property and that he would not allow them to hang him.
Tibeats and his friends went away, but nobody cut the rope. Solomon was left standing with his hands tied and the noose still around his neck, and the sun grew hotter.
Through the long afternoon people watched from a distance, but none of them dared to help. Solomon was thirsty, his arms were numb, and he began to wonder whether anyone would come at all.
In the late afternoon Ford rode in and saw what had happened. He cut the rope himself, took the noose from Solomon's neck, and helped him to the house.
That evening Solomon told Ford everything, and Ford listened quietly. He said that Solomon had been right to defend himself, but he feared what Tibeats would do next.
The next morning, back at the weaving house, Tibeats attacked Solomon with a hatchet. Solomon caught his arm, took the hatchet from him, and ran.
Tibeats called for the hounds, and a group of men on horses joined the hunt. Solomon ran for the swamp, because he knew that water would hide his scent.
Solomon waded for hours through the dark water, among tall cypress trees draped with moss. He could hear the hounds baying on the shore, but they could not follow him there.
Night fell, and the swamp filled with strange noises. Mosquitoes bit him without mercy, and the cold crept through his wet clothes, so he could not sleep.
In the morning Solomon saw that the water was full of snakes, and that alligators lay on the banks. He learned to move slowly and to watch every step.
After a day and a night in the swamp, Solomon found his way to open ground. He walked towards Ford's house, tired, hungry, and covered in mud.
Ford met him at the door, listened to the story, and gave him food and a place to sleep. For the first time in many hours, Solomon felt safe.
Tibeats soon arrived with his men and dogs and demanded that Solomon be handed over. Ford refused, and the two men argued angrily at the gate.
To keep Solomon out of Tibeats' reach, Ford arranged for him to work for a while for his brother-in-law, Peter Tanner. Solomon walked there with a note, and he was grateful.
Tanner was a much harder man than Ford, and the discipline on his farm was strict. Solomon worked there for some months and came to see how much kinder Ford had been.
In the end Solomon was sold again, this time to a planter named Edwin Epps. Epps lived on Bayou Boeuf, and he was a very different man from Ford.
Solomon was taken to Epps's plantation on Bayou Boeuf, in the cotton country of Louisiana. He did not know it yet, but he would stay there for about ten years.
Edwin Epps was a hard planter who drank heavily and was quick to use the whip. He believed that he could do whatever he liked with the people he owned.

On the plantation Solomon met the others who worked there: old Uncle Abram, Aunt Phebe, Wiley and a young woman named Patsey. They were kind to the newcomer, and they quietly taught him the rules of the place.
On his first day in the field Solomon was slow, for he had never picked cotton before. He soon learned that every worker had to pick about two hundred pounds a day.
At night everyone carried their cotton to the barn to be weighed. Those who had picked too little were whipped, and Solomon was warned that he would be if he did not improve.
Patsey was the fastest picker on the plantation, working with both hands and hardly looking at the plants. By watching her, Solomon slowly learned to pick enough to stay safe.
At night the people ground their own corn for supper and ate a little bacon. They slept for a few hours on a hard plank in a small cabin with no windows.
In time Solomon managed to get a violin again, and he played it in the evenings. The music did not take away his pain, but it helped him to remember that he was still himself.
On Sunday there was no work in the cotton field. The people used the day to wash and mend their clothes, to sit in the sun, and to rest as well as they could.
When Epps had been drinking, he woke everyone in the middle of the night and ordered them to dance while Solomon played. Anyone who slowed down could expect to be whipped.
The cotton year began in spring, when the fields were ploughed with mules. Then the seed was sown in long, straight rows that stretched to the edge of the woods.
In early summer the young plants had to be cleared of weeds by hand. Everyone worked in long lines with hoes, row after row, under a sun that grew hotter every week.
In late summer the cotton bolls opened, and the whole field turned white. From dawn until dusk everyone bent over the rows and picked as fast as they could.
Skilled pickers used both hands and never stopped moving. The dry cotton plants cut their fingers, and the long sack grew heavier with every hour.
Each night the cotton was weighed and stored in the barn. Later the machine called the gin took out the seeds, and the cotton was pressed into heavy bales.
The bales were carried by steamboat to New Orleans, and from there to cloth mills in the North and in England. Solomon sometimes thought of the shirts that his cotton would become.
Nobody could leave the plantation without a written pass from the master. Riders called patrols rode the roads at night, and they stopped and punished anyone who had no paper.
For a time Epps made Solomon carry a whip in the field and keep the others working. Solomon cracked it close to them but would not strike, and he hoped that Epps would not notice.
Solomon never let anyone know that he could read and write. He knew that on the plantation a person who could read was thought dangerous, and might be sold farther away.
Solomon decided that the way to stay alive was to say little, work hard and keep a secret hope. He believed that some chance would come, if he could only live long enough to see it.
Patsey was a young woman of about twenty, cheerful, quick and proud of her work. She was the best cotton picker on the plantation, but in that place her skill brought her more trouble than praise.
Epps's attention to Patsey made his wife, Mary, jealous and spiteful. Patsey suffered from the master for what he wanted and from the mistress for what she imagined.
Mary Epps's hatred grew so bitter that she once threw a heavy bottle at Patsey and often refused her any soap. Patsey was proud of being clean, and she felt the insult deeply.
One day, after the mistress had refused her soap, Patsey walked to a neighbouring plantation to ask for a small piece. Epps, who had been away from home, came back and found her gone.
Patsey said that she had gone only to borrow some soap, but Epps would not believe her. In a rage he ordered four stakes to be driven into the ground, and she was tied to them.
Epps ordered Solomon to whip Patsey, and Solomon, afraid, struck her lightly. When Epps threatened him, Solomon refused to go on, so Epps took the whip himself.
When it was over, the other women carried Patsey to her cabin, where she lay for days unable to stand. Solomon and the others brought her water and did what little they could.
After that terrible day Patsey was no longer the girl she had been. She stopped laughing and singing, and she moved through the fields like someone walking in a dream.
In her despair Patsey told Solomon that she wished to die. He answered gently that while she lived there was still some hope, and that she must not give up.
Slowly Patsey returned to her work in the field, and the other workers looked after her as well as they could. Solomon never forgot what he had seen, and it made his wish to escape even stronger.
In autumn, when the cotton had been picked, the sugar cane was ready to cut. Epps hired Solomon out to other planters, and he became skilled with the long, heavy cane knife.
The cutters worked in a long line, cutting each stalk at the base and stripping off the leaves. Then the cane was loaded onto carts and taken to the sugar mill.
At the sugar-house the cane was crushed and the juice boiled down in huge kettles. During the grinding season the work went on through the day and most of the night.
In the cane fields Solomon met workers from many plantations. Many of them had been sold from the older states, and he heard stories of homes and families they would never see again.
At Christmas the people were given a few days free from work. They put on their best clothes and ate a good supper, and in the evening there was a dance.
At Christmas Solomon was often asked to play the violin at parties given by white planters. He earned a few dollars and saw many fine houses, and the music made the time pass.
Whenever he travelled with a pass, Solomon studied the roads, the bayous and the plantations of the district. Little by little he built a map of the whole region in his mind.
Solomon hid the few dollars that he earned in a cloth beneath a plank. He knew that money might one day pay for paper, or for the carrying of a letter.
Runaways were hunted with dogs, and the free states lay more than a thousand miles to the north. Solomon knew that to run alone would end in capture or death.
Solomon decided to wait quietly for the right chance to come along. He wanted to find one person he could trust with his secret, but years went by, and no such person appeared.
The years went by in the same round of ploughing, hoeing, picking and cane cutting. Solomon counted the seasons, because counting kept him from forgetting how long he had been away.
At night Solomon lay awake and remembered the streets and the church bells of Saratoga. In his mind he saw Anne in the kitchen with the children around her.
Solomon wondered what Anne believed had become of him. He feared that she had given up hope, and that she thought he was dead.

Solomon counted the ages of Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo, and he knew that they were growing up without him. He wondered whether they remembered his face, and whether they still thought of him at all.
