In the heat of the summer, fever swept through the quarters. Epps cared only about the work that was lost, and the sick went back to the field as soon as they could stand.
As the years passed Epps drank more heavily, and he and his wife quarrelled more often. Their moods filled the house, and it was the people in the quarters who paid for them.
In a bad year the cotton crop was ruined by too much rain or by insects. Epps blamed the workers for it, and some of them were hired out to make up his loss.
Sometimes at night the others asked Solomon about the North. He told them about snow, railroads and schools where black children learned to read, and they listened, amazed.

News reached the plantation only in small scraps, passed on by visitors and travellers. Far away the argument over slavery was growing hotter, and in 1850 Congress passed a harsher law about people who ran away.
By the early 1850s Solomon had been held for about eleven years. He was still alive, he still remembered that his name was Solomon Northup, and he had not yet given up.
Solomon longed to write to his friends in New York, but he had no paper, no ink and no pen. He knew that to be caught writing would put his life in danger.
At last Solomon managed to take a single sheet of paper when nobody was looking. He hid it carefully, for if it was found, there would be no good explanation.
Solomon made ink by boiling the bark of a maple tree in a little water over a tiny fire. After some time the water turned dark and thick, and he found that it would leave a mark.
Solomon found a duck's feather and cut it into a pen with his small knife. He tried it on a piece of wood, and, to his great relief, it wrote well.
At night, by the glow of the fire, Solomon wrote a letter to his friends. He told them where he was and begged for help, and then he hid it in his clothes.
A poor white labourer named Armsby came to work for Epps. Solomon asked him if he would post the letter in the town of Marksville, and Armsby agreed for a price.
But Armsby betrayed him, and told Epps all about the letter. Epps stormed into the yard and demanded to know what Solomon had been doing.
Solomon said calmly that Armsby was lying, and that he had no friends to write to, nor any way to write. Epps believed him, and Armsby soon left the plantation.
That night Solomon burned the letter, the pen and the last of the ink so that nothing could be found. He watched the paper curl and turn black, and he felt that his hope was burning with it.
Solomon lay awake and thought how close he had come to disaster. He decided that he would never again trust anyone until he was completely sure.
In 1852 Epps decided to build a new house and hired a group of carpenters. One of them was Samuel Bass, a tall, quiet man who had come from Canada.
Bass was a plain-spoken man who had travelled widely and lived by his trade. He was not afraid to say what he thought, even in front of men who held slaves.
Solomon noticed that Bass spoke to the black workers as equals, without contempt and without fear. It was so unusual that he began to watch the carpenter very closely.
One day Bass told Epps to his face that slavery was wrong, and Epps only laughed. Solomon, who was working nearby, heard every word and was deeply moved.
Bass said that a law might allow a thing without making it right. He believed that the day would come when slavery would end, whatever Epps might think.
Epps thought that Bass was odd, but he could not deny that he was a fine carpenter. Because he needed the work done, he let the Canadian talk.

One evening Bass asked Solomon a few quiet questions, such as how long he had lived on the plantation and whether he was content. Solomon answered with great care, because he did not yet dare to trust him.
Solomon weighed the risk very carefully for several long days. If he was wrong, he might be killed, but Bass was the first white man in eleven years to speak openly against slavery.
Bass told of his wanderings from Canada through many states and his many different jobs. He said that he had never owned a person, and that he never would.
At last Solomon decided to take the risk and speak to Bass. He waited only for a quiet moment when nobody else was near, and he prayed that he was right.
One quiet evening, when nobody else was near, Solomon asked Bass whether he could keep a secret. Bass looked at him steadily and said that he could.
Solomon told Bass his real name and the whole story, from Saratoga to Washington, and from the pen to the plantation. He spoke quietly and in order, and Bass did not once interrupt him.
Bass was deeply shaken by what he had heard. He told Solomon that he believed every word, and that he would do everything he could to help.
Bass warned that helping a slave to prove he was free would be dangerous for him as well. If Epps and his neighbours found out, he would be driven away, or worse.
Bass asked for the names of friends who might help, and Solomon gave him two. They were Parker and Perry, merchants in Saratoga, who had known him for years.
They agreed to be very careful, and never to speak of the matter where anyone could hear. In public Bass would treat Solomon like any other worker.
That night Bass wrote a letter to Parker and Perry in Saratoga. He told them where Solomon was and begged them to send help and proof of his freedom.
Bass posted the letter at the post office in Marksville. It would take weeks to reach New York, and there was nothing that Solomon could do but wait.
That night Solomon lay awake for many hours, thinking about the future. After eleven years he had a friend who knew the truth, and he found that hope was almost as hard to bear as despair.
Bass promised that if there was no answer by Christmas, he would travel north himself in the spring. He would find Solomon's friends in Saratoga, and he would bring them back.
At last the new house was finished, and Bass packed his tools and left for Marksville. He promised to come back, and Solomon watched him until he was out of sight.
The picking season began again, and Solomon counted the weeks. A letter would take a long time to reach New York, and an answer would take just as long to come back.
In Saratoga the letter reached Parker and Perry, who were astonished to learn that Solomon was alive. They remembered him well, and they took the letter at once to his wife.
Anne read the letter and wept with joy and with fear. After so many years of silence, she and the children learned that Solomon was alive, and that he needed their help.
Anne took the letter to Henry B Northup, a lawyer at Sandy Hill. His family had once owned Solomon's father, and he agreed to help at once.
Henry studied the law and found an act of 1840 that could help. It allowed the governor of New York to send an agent to bring home a free citizen who had been kidnapped.
Henry went around Saratoga and collected sworn statements from many of Solomon's neighbours. Each of them said that Solomon had been born free and had lived among them for years.
Henry took the papers to Albany, where Governor Washington Hunt gave him official authority to bring Solomon home. Winter was setting in, and Henry prepared to leave at once.
In Louisiana Christmas came with its three free days, but Bass did not appear. Solomon played the violin for the dancing, and every few minutes he looked towards the road.
Christmas passed without any news, and in the new year Solomon went back to the cotton field almost without hope. He wondered whether Bass had forgotten him, or whether the letter had been lost.
Henry set out from the snowy north with his papers in a leather bag. His first stop was Washington, where he asked for help from men in authority.
From Washington Henry travelled on by train and by steamboat down the Mississippi. It was a long journey in winter, and he spent the hours going over his papers.
In New Orleans Henry asked the way to Bayou Boeuf. He was told that he must first go to Marksville, the seat of the parish, and put his case to the law there.
Henry went on by steamer up the Red River. The banks were lined with swamps and with cotton fields, and he knew that Solomon had once passed along the same river.
At Marksville Henry met a local lawyer named John P Waddill. Waddill listened to the story and agreed to help him bring Solomon's case before the court.
Waddill explained that Louisiana law protected owners, so Henry must prove that Solomon was free. He must act through the court, and not by force.
Waddill drew up a petition asking the court to order the sheriff to take Solomon from Epps. The judge read it, was satisfied with the evidence, and signed the order.
The sheriff and Henry set out for Bayou Boeuf in a carriage, carrying the court's order. Henry wanted to find Solomon quietly in the field rather than go first to the house.
They followed the road along the bayou and asked the way of people they met. At last they came to the edge of Epps's land, where a group of workers was picking cotton in the field.
On the third of January 1853 the carriage stopped by the roadside. Henry and the sheriff stepped down and began to walk across the field towards the line of workers.
Two strangers walked across the cotton field towards the workers. Solomon, who had learned never to stare at white visitors, went on picking and did not look up.
One of the strangers asked the man his name, and Solomon answered that it was Platt. The stranger looked at him closely and asked whether he knew him.
Solomon suddenly knew the man, who was Henry B Northup, the lawyer from Sandy Hill. Henry called him by his true name, and Solomon could not speak, and then he wept.
Epps hurried across the field, red with anger, and demanded to know what the strangers wanted. The sheriff showed him the court's order and told him that Platt was a free man named Solomon Northup.
Epps raged and said that he had bought Platt honestly and would not give him up. But the law was plain, the sheriff stood firm, and there was nothing that Epps could do to stop them.
Solomon was told that he could go at once. He had almost nothing to take with him, only a few old clothes and the violin that he had played for so many years.
Patsey ran after him, weeping, and clung to him. Epps ordered her back, and Solomon, in great sorrow, could do nothing to help her.
The others stood in a group in front of the cabins and watched. Some of them called out blessings, but none of them could follow, and Solomon never saw them again.
Epps stood at the gate and shouted angrily as the carriage pulled away. Solomon looked back until the plantation had disappeared behind the trees.
In Marksville a judge heard the evidence and declared that Solomon was a free man. The legal papers were completed, and at last Solomon held a paper that no one could take away.
Solomon and Henry went down the Red River and the Mississippi to New Orleans. For the first time in twelve years Solomon travelled as a free passenger, and nobody held a whip over him.
In New Orleans Solomon walked through the streets where he had once been sold. He saw the wharf where the brig Orleans had landed him in chains, and he looked at it as a free man.
In Washington Henry and Solomon found James Burch, the dealer who had held Solomon in the pen. Burch was arrested, and he was charged with the crime of kidnapping.
In court Burch claimed that he had bought Solomon honestly. The court would not accept a black man's word against a white man's, so the case collapsed and Burch went free.
From Washington they travelled north by train through towns covered in snow. Solomon, who had not been home for twelve years, could think of nothing else.
In January 1853 Solomon at last came home to his family in the north. Anne and the children were waiting, and they had grown up, and a little grandson had been named Solomon Northup after him.
Solomon learned what had happened while he was gone. His mother had died, his children had grown into adults, and many people had given him up for dead.
With the help of a writer named David Wilson, Solomon put his story into a book. He dedicated it to Harriet Beecher Stowe, who had written a famous novel against slavery.
The book was published in 1853 and sold many thousands of copies. Solomon spoke at meetings in the northern states, but none of the men who had stolen him was ever punished.
Today, people around the world still read Solomon Northup's story. It is one of the clearest and most truthful accounts of slavery, and it reminds us that freedom belongs to everyone.
C1C2: In 1853 a book appeared in New York whose title said exactly what had happened to its author, and the whole country began to talk about it. Solomon Northup had been born free, yet he was kidnapped in 1841 and forced to live as a slave in Louisiana for twelve years. A local writer named David Wilson helped him to put the story on paper, and Northup swore that every word of it was true.

Solomon Northup was born in July 1808 in the small town of Minerva, in the hills of New York State, and he was free from the first day of his life. His father, Mintus, had once been a slave in a family that bore the same name, but when his master died he was set free by the terms of the will. Solomon was proud of that fact, and he recalled his father as an honest, respected man who worked hard and never left his family hungry.

Slavery was still lawful in New York when Mintus was young, and he had belonged to a family of landowners named Northup in the north of the state. When his master died, the old man’s will gave him his freedom, and he took the family’s name as his own. It was a name his son would carry through twelve years of bondage, and the family that gave it would one day help to bring him home.

Mintus believed in education, and he taught his son to read, write and work with figures, which few free Black families could afford to do in those years. Solomon grew up working the land beside his father and learning, by example, what honest labour and self-respect looked like. Those lessons in reading and writing would one day matter more than either of them could have imagined.

The violin was Solomon’s great delight, and in the long evenings after farm work he taught himself tune after tune until his playing was known across the hills. Neighbours sent for him to play at weddings, harvest suppers and winter dances, and they paid him with food, thanks and the occasional coin. He could not have guessed that the same gift, which brought him so many friends, would one day bring him a stranger’s flattery and a trap.

Farm work in the hills paid little in winter, so Solomon found jobs on the Champlain Canal, where he learned to steer great rafts of timber through locks and along crowded channels. The work was hard and sometimes dangerous, but it taught him patience, balance and the habit of thinking several steps ahead. One season it even carried him north into Canada, and the long journey showed him how large the world was beyond his hills.

In the autumn of 1829 Solomon’s father died, and the family mourned a man who had risen from slavery to respect in his community. A few weeks later, on Christmas Day, Solomon married Anne Hampton, a young woman of quiet strength whom he would love for the rest of his life. They started married life with little money but with steady hands, a good name and every confidence that hard work would be enough.

For several years Solomon farmed a small plot of land and took any honest work he could find, while Anne’s cooking became so well known that the neighbours begged her to prepare their feasts. Three children were born to them in those years, Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo, and the house was never quiet. Solomon later wrote that he had been happy in those days, though poor, because everything he loved was gathered under one roof.

In 1834 the family left the farm and moved to Saratoga Springs, a fashionable town where wealthy visitors from every part of the country came each summer to drink the mineral water. Solomon found steady work at the great hotels and on building sites, including the new railroad, while Anne cooked in the hotel kitchens and her reputation grew. They were a respected family with many friends, and the children went to school and had every hope of a good future.

By the spring of 1841 Solomon Northup was thirty-two years old, a husband and father with a good name, a trade in his hands and a violin that made him welcome in any company. He loved his wife, his three children and his work, and in the evenings the house was full of laughter and music. Nothing in the quiet streets of Saratoga warned him that two strangers were about to walk into his life and take everything from it.

Late in March 1841, as Solomon walked along a Saratoga street, two well-dressed strangers stopped him and introduced themselves as Brown and Hamilton. They were polite, easy in manner and apparently prosperous, and they spoke with obvious admiration about his skill with the violin. Solomon, who loved to be asked to play, was flattered and curious, and he agreed to listen to what they had to say.

They explained that they belonged to a travelling circus company, that the company was about to give a series of shows in Washington, and that they needed a musician of his quality. The pay was generous: a dollar for each day he worked and three dollars for every evening he played. Their only request was that he leave without delay, so that the circus would not have to wait for its musician.

Solomon would have liked to ask Anne’s advice, but she and the children were away from Saratoga for the spring, and the two men were in a hurry to be gone. He turned the offer over for only a short time, for the money was good, the journey sounded like an adventure, and he saw no reason to doubt men who spoke so kindly. He agreed to go, certain that he would be back home with his earnings in his pocket before the spring was over.

Solomon packed a small bundle of clothes and said goodbye to the house, thinking only of the few weeks of easy work ahead. Then he climbed into the strangers’ carriage, and the three men set off along the road to Albany with the horses stepping briskly in the spring air. It never occurred to him, as Saratoga fell behind, that he was looking at it for the last time in twelve years.

From Albany the party travelled down the Hudson River to New York City, where Solomon looked out at crowded docks, tall ships and streets that seemed never to sleep. Brown and Hamilton treated him with great friendliness, paying for his meals and speaking cheerfully of the shows that lay ahead. Their kindness was so smooth and so constant that he never thought to ask why two circus men should spend so much on a violin player they had only just met.

Before leaving New York, Brown and Hamilton suggested that it would be sensible for Solomon to carry proof of his freedom, since they would soon be passing through states where slavery was lawful. He went with them to the Custom House, where an official took down the facts of his birth and issued a certificate declaring him a free citizen of New York. Solomon folded the paper carefully and put it away, thinking of it as a shield that no one could take from him.

They crossed the river by ferry and went south by train through the fields and towns of New Jersey, then on through Philadelphia and Baltimore. The journey felt to Solomon like a holiday, with Brown and Hamilton laughing and joking in the seat beside him and each mile bringing the promise of good pay. Behind the cheerful talk, however, the two men were taking him steadily and quietly towards a place where a free Black man had very little protection.

They reached Washington in April, when the whole city was draped in black for President William Henry Harrison, who had died only a month after taking office. Brown and Hamilton took rooms at a hotel and paid Solomon part of his wages in advance, an act that seemed to prove how honest they were. Solomon, who had expected to find the circus already at work, was told that it would arrive in a few days and that meanwhile he could rest and enjoy the sights.

While they waited for the circus to arrive, Solomon explored the city, walking up the broad avenues and gazing at the white dome of the Capitol, where the laws of the republic were made. It was a splendid sight, and for a moment it made him proud of a country that called itself free. He did not know, as he stood there, that very soon he would be locked in a cell within sight of the very same building.

On 10 April 1841 the funeral of the dead President brought the whole capital into the streets, and Solomon pressed into the crowd with Brown and Hamilton to watch. Soldiers marched with reversed arms, muffled drums kept a slow beat, and the long procession of carriages and mourners stretched farther than he could see. It was the grandest spectacle of his life, and he watched it as a free man among strangers, never suspecting that his freedom had almost run out.

That evening the three men dined together and drank wine, and soon afterwards Solomon was seized by a sickness so sudden and so heavy that he could hardly climb the stairs to his room. What followed came back to him only in pieces: a pain in his head, strange faces leaning over him, and voices that seemed to come from a great distance. After that there was nothing but darkness, and he came to believe that his wine had been drugged.

Solomon woke slowly, with a splitting headache, to find himself sitting on the cold floor of a small dark cell. His wrists were bound in handcuffs, a heavy chain ran from his ankles to a ring in the floor, and when he searched his pockets he found that his money and his free papers had been taken. For a long moment he could not believe that any of it was real, and he told himself that someone would soon come and put things right.

When Solomon finally understood what had been done to him, Brown and Hamilton were nowhere to be found. Everything he knew about them, from the flattering offer in Saratoga to the cheerful journey south, now looked like a single carefully built trap. He came to believe that they had planned it from the start, and that the kind words, the paid meals and the advance wages had all been the price of his trust.

At last the door opened, and a slave dealer named James Burch came in with a jailer at his side and told Solomon coldly that he was a runaway slave from Georgia whose name was Platt. Solomon answered at once that he was a free man from Saratoga, that he had a wife and children in New York, and that he had been kidnapped. Burch only shook his head, and it dawned on Solomon, with a creeping fear, that nothing he could say would be believed.

Burch and his jailer, Ebenezer Radburn, forced Solomon down and beat him, first with a wooden paddle that broke in two, and then with a whip of knotted cords. Solomon cried out that he was a free man, and each time he said it the blows grew harder. The beating ended only when he was too weak to speak, and he lay on the floor knowing that he had learned something terrible.

Before he left, Burch warned Solomon in a flat, unhurried voice that he would be killed if he ever again told anyone that he was free, and that no one would trouble to ask what had become of him. Solomon believed him, for the man spoke like someone who had said those words before. From that hour the truth about his name and his home became a secret that he must guard as jealously as his life.

By day the prisoners were allowed into a small yard enclosed by a high wall, and from it Solomon could see, rising above the roofs, the white dome of the Capitol. The sight was almost unbearable, for the building that stood for liberty and law looked down on the place where he was held. He understood, with bitter clarity, that the nation’s capital was also a market in which people were bought and sold.

Solomon was not the only person held in the pen, for men and women were brought in and taken out at all hours, and most of them were waiting to be shipped to the markets of the South. They spoke in low voices of the husbands, wives and children they were being forced to leave, and of the cruelty they expected to meet in the cotton and cane country. Listening to them, Solomon understood that his own misfortune was one small part of a vast and well-organised trade.

Among the captives was a woman named Eliza, who sat day after day with her two children, a boy named Randall and a girl named Emily, held close against her. She told Solomon that she had once been promised her freedom, and that she had trusted the promise, yet now she and her children were to be sold. Her grief was so deep and so constant that even the guards, who had seen such sorrow many times, sometimes looked away.

Night after night Solomon lay awake on the hard floor and thought of Anne and the children, wondering what they believed had become of him and how long they would wait. He searched his mind for any way of sending word to New York, but he had no pen, no paper and no friend he could trust, and every plan ended at the same locked gate. Then, one night, the door opened and he learned that he was not to stay in Washington.

In the middle of the night the guards roused the captives, fastened their chains and led them out into the dark street, where Burch was waiting with a carriage. They were driven through the sleeping city towards the river, and Solomon, twisting round in his seat, watched the lamps of the Capitol grow small behind him. He wondered whether any person in all that great city knew where he was, and he was certain that none did.

At the river a steamboat was waiting, and the captives were taken aboard and carried down the Potomac through the long dark hours. The other passengers strolled about the deck, talked, laughed and played cards, and not one of them stopped to ask why a group of chained men and women sat huddled below. It was a lesson that Solomon never forgot: that an injustice done in plain sight can become so ordinary that people no longer see it.

From the end of the river journey a train carried them on towards Richmond, in Virginia, rattling through woods, tobacco fields and small stations where nobody seemed to be in any hurry. Burch sat close by and kept his eyes on his captives, while the other passengers looked out of the windows and left the chained people alone. Solomon kept silent, remembering the beating, and silently promised himself that he would find a better moment to speak.

In Richmond the captives were locked in another slave pen, a plain building with a yard where more men, women and children were waiting to be sent south. The city was then one of the busiest centres of the slave trade in the country, and shiploads of people left it every season for the markets of New Orleans. Solomon, who had once thought of the South as a faraway place, now understood that he was being carried into the heart of it.

In the Richmond pen Solomon met two men, Robert and Arthur, who told him in whispers that they, too, had been free before they were seized and sold. As the three men compared their stories they found that their misfortunes were alarmingly alike. It was a small comfort to have someone to confide in, but it was also a grim discovery that such crimes were not rare.

One morning the captives were marched to the river and put aboard the brig Orleans, a trading ship that was bound for the port of New Orleans. Below deck the men and women were kept apart and chained at night in a hold that was crowded, airless and foul. Solomon, lying in the dark with the timbers creaking around him, felt every wave carry him farther from Saratoga and from everyone who loved him.

Once the ship was at sea, Solomon, Robert and Arthur began to plan in whispers how they might seize it from the captain and the crew. Solomon, who had spent years among boats and rafts, thought that the three of them might manage the brig if they could first overcome the sailors. The plan was desperate and dangerous, but it was the first hope that any of them had felt since they were captured.

Before the plan could be put into action, smallpox broke out in the crowded hold, and the disease spread from one captive to the next. Robert fell ill first, and soon afterwards Solomon himself was seized by fever and lay burning in the dark, too weak to lift his head. For days the plot was forgotten, and the only thing that mattered was whether they would live.

Robert did not recover, and one grey morning the sailors carried his body on deck and dropped it into the sea, without a prayer or a stone to mark the place. Solomon slowly regained his strength, but the plan to take the ship had died with his friend, and neither he nor Arthur had the heart to speak of it again. He lay in the hold with a feeling of hopelessness he had never known.

At last the Orleans turned into the mouth of the Mississippi and made its slow way up the wide brown river, between flat green banks and a sky heavy with heat. The city at the end of the voyage, New Orleans, was the largest slave market in the country, and Solomon knew that his fate would now be decided by whoever offered the highest price. He stepped ashore still weak from his illness, still in the chains that had bound him since Washington.

The captives were marched from the wharf, past towering piles of cotton bales and warehouses full of sugar, to a walled slave pen in the heart of the city. It belonged to a dealer named Theophilus Freeman, who walked along the line and looked them over as a farmer might look over cattle. For Solomon there was no mistaking what the cotton bales on the wharf were worth, or what the people beside them cost.

Freeman had the captives washed, shaved and dressed in new clothes, so that they would look strong, healthy and worth a high price to a buyer. He entered Solomon in his book under the name Platt, the name that Burch had invented, and Solomon, remembering the paddle and the whip, was too frightened to correct him. In that moment the man whom Saratoga had known for thirty-two years was quietly replaced by a stranger.

Every morning Freeman had the captives drawn up in the yard and made to walk briskly, hold their heads high and dance, so that watching buyers would think them strong and cheerful. Solomon was handed a violin and told to play for the dancers, and he obeyed with a heavy heart. It was the cruellest use that anyone had ever made of the one gift he loved best.

Planters and merchants came through the pen every day, feeling arms and legs, looking into mouths, ordering the men to walk and run, and asking what work each person could do. Solomon, who knew that a buyer who valued his skills might treat him better than one who did not, answered carefully and honestly. It was a humiliating performance, and it was the only influence that he had over his own future.

One day a buyer came who wanted a boy, and Randall was pulled from his mother’s arms and led towards the gate. Eliza fell on her knees, begged Freeman to keep her children with her, and promised to work twice as hard for any master who would take them all. Her cries rang through the pen, and not a person in the yard, whether captive or free, could pretend that he had not heard them.

Freeman, irritated that her weeping was bad for business, answered her pleading with angry threats and told her to be silent or she would be made to regret it. But Eliza’s sorrow was stronger than her fear, and she went on crying quietly for hours and then for days, until her voice was hoarse. Solomon, who had been taught that the truth would be punished, learned also that grief could be.

One afternoon a planter named William Ford, a Baptist preacher from the country of the Red River, came to the pen to buy workers for his farm. He was a quiet, serious man, and the sight of Eliza’s grief visibly troubled him, though he did not pause in the business of buying. When the bargaining ended, he had paid Freeman a considerable sum for Solomon and for Eliza, and the two were told that they now belonged to him.

When it was time to leave, Eliza was taken away with Ford, but her small daughter Emily was kept behind in Freeman’s pen, and the child clung to her mother’s dress until a man pulled her loose. Eliza turned and stretched out her arms, and the cry she gave as she was led away stayed in Solomon’s ears for the rest of his life. He never saw either of her children again, and he never heard what became of them.

From New Orleans Ford took his new workers up the Mississippi by steamboat and then turned into the Red River, whose banks were lined with cotton fields and cypress swamps. On the way he spoke to Solomon courteously and plainly, as a man might speak to an employee, which was quite unlike anything Solomon had met since leaving New York. Yet the kindness was hard to enjoy, for each hour carried him farther from home, and Ford, however gentle, was still his owner.

After a last long ride through the silent pines, they reached Ford’s home, a plain house in a clearing, where his wife came out to greet them with a kindness that Solomon had not expected. He was given a supper of corn and bacon and shown to a cabin close to the sawmill, where he lay down on a pallet and listened to the night. The simple comfort made him weep, because it reminded him of everything he had lost.

William Ford was a Baptist minister, and on Sundays he gathered the people on his farm and read the Bible aloud to them under the trees. Judged by the standards of that country he was a gentle and fair master, and Solomon, who had good reason to compare, always spoke of him with respect. Yet it was a bitter truth that the best of masters still held men and women as property, and that his kindness could not undo the wrong.

Solomon was set to work at Ford’s sawmill, where the great pines of the district were hauled in, trimmed and sawn into planks and beams. His years among the timber rafts of New York had taught him how wood behaved and how heavy loads could be moved, and he worked quickly, quietly and with evident skill. Ford noticed, and Solomon, who had expected nothing but harshness, began to think that his situation might be less terrible than he had feared.

Ford had agreed to supply a large order of planks to a distant builder, but the road was deep sand and the wagons sank to their axles. Every journey cost him days of work and several exhausted animals, and the contract seemed likely to swallow most of his profit. It was a problem of exactly the kind that Solomon had spent his youth solving on the canals.

Solomon ventured to tell Ford that in New York he had floated timber on rafts for years, and he suggested lashing the planks together and sending them down the creek. Ford was doubtful, for the creek was winding and shallow, and no one had ever tried to use it in that way. But he was an open-minded man, and after a moment’s thought he told Solomon to try.

Solomon built the first raft with his own hands, lashing the planks together with the care of a man who had done it a hundred times, and then took it down the winding creek himself, steering with a long pole. The journey was slow and tricky, but the raft swung round each bend as he had hoped, and the planks arrived faster and more cheaply than they could have done by road. Ford was delighted, and for a short while Solomon felt something close to pride.

Ford praised Solomon warmly in front of his neighbours, telling them that Platt was the cleverest man he owned, and for some weeks Solomon was treated with a consideration that few in his position ever knew. He was grateful, and he worked well, but every compliment in this place was spoken to a man who was somebody’s property. No amount of kindness could change that, and he never allowed himself to forget it.

After a time Ford decided to take up a new business on Bayou Boeuf, a slow, winding stream that ran through some of the richest farming country in Louisiana. He moved his household there, with its wagons, tools and workers, and took Solomon with him to build and mend whatever the new place required. Solomon watched the pine forest fall away and saw, for the first time, the broad cotton fields and cane brakes of the low country.

Ford, it turned out, was deeply in debt, and to meet what he owed he was forced to sell Solomon to a carpenter named John Tibeats, who had been working on the new buildings. Ford kept a mortgage of four hundred dollars on Solomon, which meant that he still held a legal claim on him, but the man himself now belonged to Tibeats. Ford told Solomon quietly that he was sorry to do it, and Solomon, who had learned to read men’s faces, believed him.

John Tibeats was a small, hot-tempered man with a bitter tongue, and he could not bear to be corrected, least of all by someone he owned. Solomon was the better carpenter by a wide margin, and Tibeats knew it, which made him all the more spiteful. He found fault with everything Solomon did, however well it was done, and the days grew steadily more dangerous.

Solomon and Tibeats set about building a weaving house, a long low shed for the looms, and from morning to night Tibeats found something to curse. A young man named Chapin, who served as Ford’s overseer on that plantation and was known for his fairness, watched the work from a distance and kept his opinions to himself. Solomon sensed that sooner or later the quarrel would come to a head, and that Chapin would be there when it did.

One morning Tibeats flew into a rage over a box of nails, although Solomon had done exactly as he had been told, and no argument could calm him. He snatched up a whip and told Solomon that he would be taught a lesson he would not forget. For the first time since his capture, Solomon felt something stronger than fear stirring inside him.

When Tibeats raised the whip, Solomon grabbed the other end of it, and the two men struggled together beside the half-built wall until the stronger one prevailed. Solomon wrenched the whip away and, in the heat of his anger, used it on his master, who howled for help and begged to be released. It was a reckless act, and he knew as he did it that it might cost him his life.

Tibeats limped away towards a neighbouring plantation, and before long he came hurrying back with two other white men and a length of rope. They had not come to talk, and Solomon saw from their faces that they meant to punish him in the cruellest way they could. He could not run, for there was nowhere to run to, and he could only stand and wait.

The three men pinned Solomon down, tied his hands behind him and slipped a noose over his head, while Tibeats spat out his orders in a shaking voice. They dragged him to the nearest tree and began to fling the free end of the rope over a high branch. Solomon, who had always believed that a man should be able to speak in his own defence, found that nobody would let him say a word.

At that moment Chapin, the overseer, came running from the house with a pistol in each hand and ordered the men to stop. He reminded them, in a voice that left no room for argument, that Solomon belonged to Ford, that Ford held a mortgage on him, and that nobody would be allowed to hang him on that plantation. Solomon understood that he had been saved by the value of his own body, and not by the justice of his cause.

Tibeats and his friends went away muttering threats, but nobody cut the rope, and Solomon was left standing under the tree with his hands tied and the noose still loosely round his neck. The sun climbed higher, the ground grew hot under his feet, and the cord cut deeper into his wrists with every passing hour. He tried to keep his mind steady by thinking of Anne and the children, but the pain made even their faces hard to hold.

All through the long afternoon men and women peered from the doors and corners of the plantation, but none dared to come near, for they knew too well what happened to those who defied a white man’s will. Solomon was desperately thirsty, his hands had turned numb and his legs trembled with the effort of standing. He began to wonder whether it was possible to be forgotten by the whole world while still in plain view of it.

In the late afternoon Ford rode in, saw at a glance what had been done, and cut the rope himself with a sharp knife, his hands shaking with anger. He lifted the noose from Solomon’s neck, loosened the cords around his wrists and led him gently towards the house. The hours of suffering were over, but Solomon would never forget that his life had been judged to be worth just four hundred dollars.

That evening, in the quiet of Ford’s house, Solomon told the whole story from beginning to end, and Ford listened without interrupting once. He said that a man who is attacked has every right to defend himself, but that Tibeats was a vengeful person and that the trouble was far from over. Solomon was comforted by the kindness of his words, though he knew that no kindness could change the law.

The next morning Solomon went back to the weaving house, as he had been ordered, and Tibeats was waiting for him with a hatchet in his hand and murder in his face. Solomon caught the man’s arm as the blow came down, tore the weapon from his grasp and ran, knowing that this time there would be no excuse for him if he were caught. Behind him, as he crossed the field with his heart pounding, he could hear Tibeats shouting for the dogs.

Tibeats called for the hounds, and soon a group of men on horseback had joined the hunt, with the dogs giving tongue as they cast about for his trail. Solomon ran for the nearest swamp, remembering that water carries no scent, and plunged into it without a backward glance. It was a desperate chance, and he took it because the only alternative was the rope.

For hours Solomon waded through black, knee-deep water among tall cypress trees draped in grey moss, feeling his way over roots and unseen holes. From somewhere behind him came the baying of the hounds, now near, now far, but the water had done its work and they could not find his trail. The silence of the swamp was heavy and unbroken, and for the moment he was almost glad of it.

Night fell, and the swamp came alive with the shrill cries of insects, the croaking of frogs and the splash of creatures moving in the dark. Mosquitoes swarmed around him, wet clothes clung to his body, and the chill crept into his bones, so that sleep was impossible. He sat with his back against a trunk and waited for dawn, listening for the sound of men.

When daylight reached the swamp it showed him water moccasins gliding between the roots and alligators lying like fallen logs along the banks. Solomon discovered that the creatures did not trouble a man who moved slowly and watched where he put his feet, and he drew a grim comfort from the thought that they were less dangerous than Tibeats. Even so, every step he took in that dark and tangled place was a gamble, and he took each one with care.

After a day and a night in the swamp, Solomon found his way to open ground, and in the grey light of dawn he saw the roof of Ford’s house in the distance. He was cold, hungry, covered in mud and scratched by thorns, but he had no thought of going anywhere else, for Ford was the only white man in Louisiana who had ever shown him pity. He walked on very slowly, afraid to hurry lest he should fall and be unable to rise again.

Ford met him at the door, took one look at his state and ordered food to be brought at once, and then he listened gravely while Solomon told the story of the swamp. He gave him a bed in the loft of an outbuilding, covered him with a blanket and promised that nobody would harm him while he was on the plantation. For the first time in many hours Solomon felt safe, and he slept like a man who has been given back a small piece of his life.

Tibeats soon arrived with his men and dogs and demanded that Solomon be handed over to him at once, and for a long while the two men argued across the gate, Tibeats loud and Ford quiet. Ford reminded him that the mortgage still gave him a claim and refused to let the man be taken, though he could not punish Tibeats for the attempt to kill him. Solomon, listening from the loft, understood that the law which guarded Ford’s property would never guard his own life.

To keep Solomon out of Tibeats’s reach, Ford arranged for him to work for a time for his brother-in-law, Peter Tanner, who owned a farm some miles away. Solomon walked there carrying a note, with a heavy heart and a mixture of gratitude and dread. He was leaving the only protector he had in Louisiana, and he had no idea what kind of man would be his master now.

Peter Tanner was a far harder man than Ford, and the discipline on his farm was strict and quick to punish, so that Solomon, who had been grateful for Ford’s mildness, now understood how rare it was. He worked there for some months, saying little, keeping out of trouble and watching how the other workers were treated. It was a lesson in how much a person’s fate depends upon the character of the man who happens to own him.

In the end the matter was settled in the way such matters always were, with a bargain and a signature, and in about 1843 Solomon was sold to a planter named Edwin Epps. Epps lived on Bayou Boeuf, in the heart of the cotton country, and he was a very different man from either Ford or Tanner. Solomon, who had already learned that a master could change his whole life, set out for the new plantation with an anxious heart.

The road to Epps’s plantation ran beside a slow brown bayou, past cotton fields as wide as lakes, rows of whitewashed cabins and groups of workers who did not look up as the wagon passed. Solomon, who was now in the heart of the cotton country, could not have guessed that he would remain on that one plantation for about ten years. The sights were new, but the feeling of being carried further and further from home was one he knew all too well.

Edwin Epps was a heavy-drinking, hard-faced planter whose temper could turn in an instant from jovial good humour to savage rage. He was quick with the whip, he took a pride in his reputation for severity, and he sincerely believed that he had a right to do whatever he pleased with the people he held. Solomon, who had met kindness in Ford and cruelty in Tibeats, saw at once that this man was more dangerous than either.

In the quarters Solomon met the others who laboured for Epps: Uncle Abram, the oldest of them, Aunt Phebe, Wiley, and a young woman named Patsey, whose quick hands and ready laugh he noticed at once. They welcomed the newcomer in the quiet, careful way of people who have little to give but their company. From them he began to learn the unwritten rules of the place, and the dangers that went with breaking each one.

On his first morning in the cotton field Solomon was given a long sack and shown how to strip the white bolls from the stalks, but his fingers were clumsy, and the hours passed more slowly than he thought possible. He soon learned that every worker was expected to bring in about two hundred pounds each day, and that anyone who fell short was punished. The rule was simple, and from that first day it governed every moment of his waking life, from the first light to the last.

At nightfall every person carried a heavy sack to the barn, where Epps weighed the day’s cotton on a scale and entered the figures in his book. Anyone whose sack fell short was whipped, and Solomon, who had been spared on that first evening, was told bluntly that he would not be spared again if he did not improve. He went to bed with the figure of two hundred pounds hanging over him like a sentence.

Patsey was the swiftest picker on the plantation, moving down the row with both hands flying and scarcely looking at the plants, and she regularly brought in far more than any of the men. Solomon watched her closely and copied her rhythm, and in the course of a few weeks he learned to reach the daily weight without being punished. It was a poor kind of success, but in that place it was the difference between safety and pain.

When the day’s picking was done, each person had to grind corn for supper, light a small fire and cook a meal of coarse cornbread and a little bacon, so that it was often late before anyone could lie down. They slept on a hard plank with a rough blanket in a cabin that had no window and hardly any furniture, and the horn that woke them came before dawn. Solomon later wrote that sleep was the only kind of freedom the quarters knew.

With a few coins that he had saved, Solomon managed in time to get a violin again, and he played it in the evenings when the day’s work was done. The music could not lift the weight of the cotton or the memory of what he had lost, but it was a means of carrying his mind away from the plantation for an hour. People gathered quietly to listen, and for a little while the cabin felt almost like a home.

Sunday was the one day of the week when the horn did not call the workers to the cotton rows, and the quarters took on a different mood, quieter and slower. People washed their clothes in the bayou, mended torn shirts, tended small matters of their own and sat in the sun to talk. It was a short, precious breathing space, and everybody knew that on Monday it would be taken away.

When Epps had been drinking, which was often, he would burst into the quarters in the middle of the night, rouse everyone from sleep and order them into the house to dance while Solomon played the violin. Anyone who flagged or stumbled could expect to feel the whip, and the music went on until the master was tired or until the first light broke. Solomon played, and he hated every note, but he knew that an exhausted person who refused would suffer far worse.

The cotton year began in the spring, when the fields were ploughed in long straight furrows behind teams of mules and the black earth was raked fine. Then the seed was dropped and covered, row after row, in lines that ran from the cabins to the edge of the woods. It was heavy, unglamorous work, and it was the first step in a year that would end in the picking sack.

In early summer the young plants had to be thinned and cleared of weeds, and the whole plantation turned out in long lines with hoes, advancing down the rows under a sun that grew fiercer every week. The work was monotonous and the heat was heavy and damp, so that sweat ran into the eyes and the hoe grew slippery in the hand. By evening every back ached and every hand was raw, yet the rows still stretched ahead as far as the eye could see.

In late summer the cotton bolls split open and the whole field turned white, as though a great snowfall had descended on the plantation. It was a beautiful sight, but it meant that the hardest season had arrived, and from the first light until dusk everyone bent over the rows and picked as fast as their hands would go. The beauty of the field, Solomon thought, was a cruel disguise for the labour it demanded.

Skilled pickers worked with both hands at once, plucking the fibre from the open bolls without a pause and dropping it into the long sack that dragged behind them along the ground. The dry, sharp husks cut the fingers until they bled, the sun burned the neck and the sack grew heavier with every hour, but no one dared to straighten up for long. Solomon discovered that the real skill lay in never pausing, since a moment’s rest was a pound lost.

Each evening the day’s cotton was weighed and stored in the barn, and when enough had been gathered it was carried to the gin house, where a machine tore the seeds from the fibre. The clean cotton was then packed under a heavy press into bales, wrapped in rough cloth and tied with rope until each one was as dense as a block of stone. Everything about the process was efficient, and almost none of the profit reached the people who had picked it.

The finished bales were loaded on steamboats that carried them down the bayou to New Orleans, and from there ships took them to the cloth mills of the North and of England. Solomon sometimes wondered whether some shirt or dress, worn in a respectable parlour in New York, had been woven from cotton that his own bleeding fingers had picked. It was a thought that connected him to his home, and it made the connection terrible.

Nobody could leave the plantation without a written pass signed by the master, and the roads were watched at night by mounted patrols whose duty was to stop any black man or woman who had no paper. Those who were caught could be whipped on the spot and returned to their owners with a note about the offence. Solomon saw that the whole district, and not only Epps, stood guard over the system, and that escape was far harder than any person from the North could imagine.

For a time Epps made Solomon carry a whip in the cotton field and drive the other workers along the rows, on the threat that he would himself be whipped if he did not. Solomon learned to crack the whip loudly and to let the tip fall a hair’s breadth away from the shoulders of the people ahead of him, and they, understanding, flinched in time. It was a miserable compromise, and he could never forgive himself for being obliged to make it.

Solomon never let anyone on the plantation suspect that he could read and write, for such a man would be thought dangerous and might be sold into a region that no letter could ever leave. It was a hard discipline, because each time he heard an owner struggling over a written order he had to hide his face and say nothing. He understood that his ignorance, carefully acted, was the cloak that kept him alive.

As the first year on the plantation closed, Solomon settled upon a plan for survival: to say little, to work well, and to keep a hidden hope burning in some corner of his heart. He told himself that sooner or later a chance would come, and that when it did, he must be alive and sound enough to take it. It was a slender hope, but through the darkest nights of the years that followed it was the only one he had.

Patsey was a young woman of about twenty, lively, quick-witted and straight-backed, with a laugh that carried across the fields. She was the best cotton picker that Epps had ever owned, and she took a quiet pride in her work. But in that house her gifts were a curse rather than a blessing, for Epps’s attention to her was constant, unwelcome and cruel.

Epps’s attention to Patsey filled his wife, Mary, with a jealous fury that she could not direct at him and so turned upon the young woman instead. Patsey suffered at the hands of the master for what he wanted and at the hands of the mistress for what she imagined, and neither of them ever thought to ask what Patsey herself wanted. There was no one to whom she could appeal, and no court that would hear her.

Mrs Epps’s hatred grew so bitter that on one occasion she hurled a heavy glass bottle at Patsey, and she refused to allow her the smallest piece of soap, although she knew that Patsey was proud of keeping herself clean. These petty cruelties were designed to wound a proud young woman, and they succeeded in doing so. Patsey endured them in silence, for she knew that any complaint would only be answered with the whip.

One day, having been refused a scrap of soap by her mistress, Patsey walked across to a neighbouring plantation, where she knew a kind woman who might spare her a piece. Epps, who had come back from town in a foul temper, found that she was missing, and he waited at the gate with the whip in his hand. When she returned, quietly and without hurry, he demanded to know where she had been.

Patsey told him truthfully that she had gone only to borrow some soap, but Epps, who was drunk and in a violent mood, would not hear her. He ordered four stakes to be driven into the ground in front of the cabins and had Patsey tied face down between them, while the others were made to stand and watch. His wife looked on from the porch, and there was no mercy in her face.

Epps ordered Solomon to take the whip and strike Patsey, and Solomon, knowing that to refuse would put his own life in danger, struck her lightly a few times, hoping to satisfy his master. But Epps saw what he was doing, threatened to kill him and demanded that he strike harder, and at that point Solomon said that he would not. Epps seized the whip himself and used it on Patsey with such violence that Solomon could scarcely bear to watch.

When it was finished, the other women lifted Patsey gently from the stakes and carried her to the cabin, where she lay for days unable to stand or to turn. Solomon and the others brought her water and wet cloths and did what little they could, for no doctor was ever called to such a place. He never lost the picture of that evening, or the feeling of his own helplessness.

After that terrible day Patsey was never again the girl whom Solomon had met on his first morning. The laughter drained out of her face, she ceased to sing in the evenings and she moved through the cotton rows like someone walking in a dream. It was a lesson in how deeply cruelty can wound a person, even when the scars cannot be seen.

In her despair Patsey told Solomon, one evening beside the bayou, that she wished she could die and be at peace. He answered gently that while she was alive there was still a chance, however small, that things might change, and that those who cared for her needed her to endure. It was a hard thing to say to someone who had so little, and he was not sure that he believed it himself.

Slowly Patsey returned to the cotton rows, and the others looked after her as well as they could, sharing food, taking some of her weight when the master was not watching and saying little. Solomon never forgot what he had witnessed, and the memory deepened his determination to find some way out of that world. He knew that every person in it, himself included, could be broken by one angry man’s will.

In the autumn, when the last of the cotton had been picked, the sugar cane stood ripe and tall in the neighbouring fields, and Epps hired Solomon out to other planters for the cutting. He soon became skilled with the long, heavy cane knife, which he learned to swing in a single clean stroke at the root of the stalk. It was savage work, but it gave him a change of scene and a small share of independence.

The cutters advanced across the field in a long line, each one chopping the stalk close to the ground, stripping the sharp leaves and tossing the cane onto a growing pile behind. Mule carts followed, loaded the stalks and carried them off to the sugar mill, where the work was only half done. It was a rhythm that Solomon learned to follow without thought, and he found that his mind could go elsewhere while his arms kept time.

At the sugar-house the cane was crushed between heavy rollers and the sweet juice was boiled down in huge kettles, in rooms full of steam and a thick, sticky smell. In the grinding season the work went on through the day and for much of the night, and men dropped into sleep on the spot whenever there was a moment’s pause. It was exhausting, but the sweetness of the air offered a strange contrast to the bitterness of the labour.

In the cane fields Solomon met workers from a dozen plantations, and in the brief pauses between tasks he listened to their stories. Many of them had been sold away from Virginia, Maryland or Kentucky, and almost all carried the memory of a parent, a husband or a child whom they would never see again. He understood that his own tragedy, though unusual in its details, was shared in substance by hundreds of people who stood beside him.

At Christmas the work was suspended for about three days, and the whole quarter was transformed, with the women in clean, bright dresses, the men in their best coats and the smell of cooking drifting from every door. There was a great supper, with meat and cakes that were seen at no other time of the year, and in the evening the dancing began. For a few hours Solomon could almost forget where he was, though he never quite forgot who he was.

At Christmas Solomon was often hired to play the violin at balls given by the planters of the neighbourhood, and he travelled from one great house to another with a pass in his pocket and the instrument under his arm. He played until dawn for guests who scarcely noticed him, was paid a few dollars at the end of the night and returned to the quarters with a sore arm and a head full of music. For those few hours it was the nearest he ever came to a life that belonged to himself.

Whenever he travelled with a pass, Solomon made a point of noticing the roads, the bayous and the plantations of the district, the names of the owners and the distances between them. Little by little he built up a map in his head of the whole region, and he stored every detail with care. He did not yet know what use it would be, but he had learned that knowledge was the one thing that nobody could take from him.

The few dollars that Solomon earned from his violin he hid in a scrap of cloth beneath a loose plank in the cabin, and he counted them in the dark when he could not sleep. He knew that money, small as the sum was, might one day buy paper, or pay for the carrying of a letter to the free states. It was a precarious treasure, and he guarded it as a miser might guard gold.

Runaways were tracked by hounds that could follow a scent through miles of marsh, and the free states lay well over a thousand miles to the north, across rivers, swamps and country where any black traveller could be stopped. Solomon had seen what happened to those who were brought back and had no wish to be one of them. He understood that flight on his own would end in capture or death, and that his only real hope lay in help from outside.

Solomon resolved to wait for the right chance and, if possible, to find one person whom he could trust with the secret of who he really was. He studied the faces of the strangers who came and went, the carriers, the peddlers, the labourers, and weighed each of them in his mind. Years went by, however, and the person he was looking for, so patiently and so carefully, did not appear.

Year followed year in the same unbroken round of ploughing, hoeing, picking and cane cutting, so that the seasons on Epps’s plantation seemed to blur into a single long summer. Solomon kept a careful count of them, because he feared that if he lost track of time he might lose himself as well. The sums he made were bitter ones, and he made them again every spring, when the planting began.

At night, when the cabin was silent but for the frogs, Solomon lay awake and walked in memory through the streets of Saratoga, past the hotels, the shops and the church with its bell. In his mind he saw Anne in the kitchen with the children gathered round her and the lamp lit on the table. It was a precious picture, and a painful one, and he returned to it every night.

Solomon wondered endlessly what Anne believed had become of him, whether she imagined him dead or lost or merely faithless, and how she had managed to care for the children on her own. He feared that she had given up hope, and that she was learning to live as though he had never existed. The thought of her grief was almost harder to endure than his own, and it came to him more often than any other.

Solomon counted up the ages of Elizabeth, Margaret and Alonzo each year and understood that the little children he had left were growing into young people he would hardly recognise. He wondered whether they remembered his face, his songs and the sound of his violin, and he feared that he would one day return to find himself a stranger in his own house. It was a thought that tormented him more than any whip, and it followed him into the field every morning.

In the damp heat of summer, fever swept through the quarters, and the sick lay shaking on their planks while the cotton waited to be picked. Epps cared for nothing except the work that was being lost, and he sent the weakest back to the field as soon as they could stand, with no medicine and little food. Solomon, who had once believed that illness was a matter for doctors, saw how little a life counted when it belonged to someone else.

As the years passed Epps drank more and more heavily, and the arguments between him and his wife grew louder and more bitter, until their moods hung over the whole plantation like weather. It was always the people in the quarters who paid for those storms, with a harsher whip, a shorter rest or the sudden cry of rage at the door at night. Solomon learned to read the signs of each coming storm and to keep out of the way for as long as he could.

In a bad year the cotton crop was ruined by too much rain or by a plague of worms, and Epps, who could not blame the weather, blamed his workers instead. To make up for what he had lost, he hired many of them out to other planters, and Solomon found himself in strange fields, among strangers, for weeks at a time. It was a reminder that his whole existence rested upon the fortunes of a man who owed him nothing.

Sometimes, at night, the others gathered round the fire and asked Solomon to tell them about the North, which to most of them was a place as unreal as the moon. He described the deep winter snow, the locomotives that hauled long trains across the country and the schools in which black children learned to read, and they listened as though to a fairy tale. He was careful, however, never to say who he really was, for even the kindest friend might talk.

News reached the plantation only in scraps, overheard from visitors on the porch or caught from a newspaper left on a rail, but Solomon gathered that the quarrel over slavery was growing hotter in the country he had left. In 1850 Congress passed a harsher Fugitive Slave Act, which made it easier to seize people who had escaped, and even some who had never been slaves. It made his own situation, if that were possible, more dangerous, for a man who had never been a slave could be seized as easily as any other.

By the early 1850s Solomon had been held for more than eleven years, and the plantation had stolen his youth, his home and his name, yet it had not extinguished his hope. He was still alive, he still remembered that he was Solomon Northup, a free man, a husband and a father, and he was biding his time. He did not know that his deliverance was already making its way towards him along a distant road.

Solomon longed to write to his friends in New York and tell them where he was, but he had no paper, no ink and no pen, and to be caught with any of them would put his life in danger. The idea haunted him, though, and he turned it over night after night, asking himself how a person might make a letter out of nothing. At last, in the stillness of one long night, he began to think that it might be done after all.

After weeks of watching and waiting, Solomon at last managed to slip a single sheet of paper from the house when nobody was looking, and he hid it inside his shirt with a heart that thudded like a drum. He knew very well that if it was found, there would be no explanation that Epps would accept, and that he might be whipped almost to death. It was the greatest risk he had run since the night in the swamp, and he did not draw a steady breath until it was done.

Solomon made his ink by boiling strips of maple bark in a little water over a tiny fire, shielding the glow with his body so that nobody would see it. After some time the liquid turned dark and thick, and when he tried it on a scrap of wood he found that it left a clear mark. It was a poor substitute for the ink of the shops, but it was enough for his purpose.

Solomon found a long feather from a duck and shaped it into a pen with his small knife, trimming the tip with the patience of a craftsman and splitting it carefully so that the ink would flow. He tried it on a piece of wood, and, to his great relief, it wrote clearly. After eleven years without so much as a pencil, the simplest of tools felt to him like a small miracle.

That night, bending close to the dying fire, Solomon wrote a letter in his best hand, telling his friends in New York that he had been kidnapped and was held on a plantation in Louisiana. He begged them to send help at once, and he wrote slowly and with enormous care, because he had only one sheet and no chance of a second attempt. When the last line was dry, he folded the letter small and hid it in the lining of his clothes.

A poor white labourer named Armsby had come to work on the plantation for a season, and Solomon, who had been looking for a messenger for years, decided to risk his secret. He offered to pay Armsby a small sum if he would carry the letter to the post office at Marksville, and Armsby, who seemed friendly and hungry for money, agreed at once. Solomon handed it over with a feeling of relief that he had not known for years.

But Armsby was not a friend, and in the hope of being paid twice he went straight to Epps and told him everything that he knew. Epps stormed into the yard, white with anger, and demanded that Solomon tell him at once who he had been writing to and what he had said. Solomon, who felt the ground open beneath him, understood that he had only a few seconds in which to save his life.

Solomon said as calmly as he could that Armsby was lying, that he had no friends to write to, no paper and no pen, and that the man had invented the story to cheat him. Epps, who had little respect for poor white labourers, thought about it and then decided to believe his own man, and Armsby soon left the plantation. It was a dangerous bluff, and it succeeded only by the narrowest of margins, as Solomon knew very well.

That night, when the others were asleep, Solomon thrust the letter into the fire, together with the pen and the last of his ink, so that no trace of his crime should remain. He watched the paper curl, glow and turn to black flakes, and he felt as though his own hope were burning with it. It was the end of the best plan he had ever made, and the loss of the only hope he had been able to build in years.

Solomon lay awake until dawn, thinking how close he had come to being sold into some farther and darker place, or beaten to death, and how a single poor man’s greed had undone years of planning. He swore to himself that he would never again trust anyone with his secret until he was quite certain that the person could be trusted. For the next few months he did nothing at all but work, keep silent and wait, as he had done so many times before.

In 1852 Epps decided to build himself a larger house, and he hired a team of carpenters to raise a new one beside it, with Solomon and others to fetch and carry. One of the carpenters was a man named Samuel Bass, who had come from Canada and now worked at Marksville, and who had a manner very different from that of the other hired men. From the moment he arrived, Solomon felt a curious sense that this stranger might be worth watching.

Samuel Bass was a plain-spoken, weather-beaten man who had wandered through many places and lived by his trade, and he had picked up the independence of mind that comes from not belonging to any one corner of the world. He said what he thought, in a tone neither loud nor timid, even in front of men who owned slaves and would not have cared to hear it. Solomon, who had been among such men for eleven years, had never heard anything like it.

Solomon noticed that Bass spoke to the black workers on the plantation plainly and as equals, without contempt and without the faint shadow of fear that other white men carried. It was so unusual in that place that Solomon began to watch the carpenter closely, noting every word and gesture. He reminded himself, sternly, that a kind surface could hide a cruel heart, and that Armsby had taught him the price of hope.

One day, as the walls of the new house rose, Bass told Epps to his face that slavery was a great wrong, and Epps, who regarded the notion as a joke, only threw back his head and laughed. But Bass did not laugh, and he went on speaking in a calm and steady voice while the planter tried to wave the matter away. Solomon, working a few yards away with his head bent, heard every word and was deeply moved.

Bass argued that a law might permit a thing without ever making it right, and that human beings who were bought and sold had the same feelings as any others, whatever the statute books said. He declared his belief that the day would come when slavery would end, whatever Epps might think or say about it. Epps replied that Bass was a dreamer, a Canadian, and a man who had never owned anything worth the trouble of defending.

Epps considered Bass a strange fellow with strange notions, but he could not deny that the man was an excellent carpenter who worked quickly, charged fairly and left no job unfinished. Since he wanted his house built, he put up with the Canadian’s opinions as a man might tolerate the weather, and the arguments between them became a kind of comic entertainment on the porch. Solomon followed each argument with the closest attention, though he never once raised his eyes from his work.

One evening, when the other workers had gone, Bass put down his tools and asked Solomon a few quiet questions about how long he had lived on the plantation and whether he was content. Solomon answered each one with great care, saying as little as he could and watching the carpenter’s face for any sign of a trap. He could not yet tell whether this was kindness or a clever kind of curiosity.

For days Solomon weighed the risk, turning it over and over in the darkness of his cabin and picturing the faces of Armsby and of Burch. If he was wrong, he might be sold, whipped or killed, and he would never have another chance, but Bass was the first white man in eleven years who had spoken openly against slavery in his hearing. It was a gamble on which everything depended, and he knew it better than anyone, as he lay there in the dark.

In the evenings Bass sometimes told of his wanderings, which had taken him from his birthplace in Canada through many states and a great variety of occupations. He spoke of the people he had met with a dry and tolerant humour, and he said that he had never owned another human being and that he never would, whatever the profits. Solomon listened carefully to every word, and he began, against all his caution, to believe him.

At last Solomon made up his mind that, whatever the danger, he would speak to Bass, for he had learned that the greatest risk of all would be to let a chance like this pass by. He waited only for a quiet moment, when Epps was away and the other workers were out of hearing, and he prayed with all his heart that he was not mistaken. It was a decision of the kind that comes only once in a life, and he felt its full weight.

One quiet evening, when nobody else was near and the only sound was the cry of the night insects, Solomon asked Bass in a low voice whether he could keep a secret that might cost them both their lives. Bass looked at him steadily for some time and then said that he could, and that he would give his word on it. It was not much to build a rescue upon, but it was enough to begin.

Then Solomon told Bass his real name and the whole story: Saratoga, Anne and the children, the two strangers, the hotel in Washington, the cell and the long years among the cotton rows. He spoke quietly and in careful order, and Bass, sitting very still beside him, did not once interrupt. When it was over, he felt as though he had set down a weight that he had been carrying for eleven years.

Bass sat silent for a long time after the story ended, and Solomon saw that the man was deeply shaken, for the story had moved him very deeply. He said that he believed every word, that he was grieved beyond words, and that he would do everything in his power to help. Solomon, who had not been believed by a single living soul for eleven years, was too moved to speak.

Bass said frankly that what they were planning would put him in danger as well, since a white man who helped a slave to gain his freedom was hated by his neighbours. If Epps and the men of the district found out, he said, he would have to answer for it. But he had made up his mind, he added, and nothing that Solomon said would persuade him to change it.

Bass asked for the names of friends who might still be willing to help after so many years, and Solomon, after a moment’s thought, gave him two: Parker and Perry, merchants in Saratoga. He described their shop and the street it stood on, and Bass committed every detail to memory. Both men understood that this small slip might become the key to the rest of Solomon’s life.

They agreed to be extremely careful, and never to speak of the matter anywhere that they might be overheard, whether in the house, the yard or the field. In public, Bass would treat Solomon exactly as he treated every other worker on the plantation, with brisk and unremarkable civility, and Solomon would play the part of a humble hand. It was a dangerous charade, and they kept it up, day after day, for as long as the building of the house lasted.

That night, at a table by candlelight, Bass wrote a letter to Parker and Perry in Saratoga, telling them that Solomon Northup was alive and held on the plantation of Edwin Epps on Bayou Boeuf. He begged them to send help and proof of his freedom without delay, writing with the plain, careful hand of a workman, and he read it through twice before he sealed it. It was, though he could not have known it, the most important letter that he would ever write.

Bass took the letter to the post office at Marksville and saw it safely sent off with the northern mail. It would take weeks to reach New York, and weeks more for an answer to return, and Solomon could do nothing but wait and go on with his work. He had waited for eleven years, he told himself, and surely he could wait a little longer.

That night Solomon lay awake with his eyes open in the darkness, unable to sleep for the first time in years because of joy rather than grief. After eleven years there was a living man outside the quarters who knew who he was, and the thought of it burned inside him like a small flame. He found, to his surprise, that hope could be almost as hard to bear as despair.

Before they parted that night Bass made a solemn promise that if no answer had arrived by Christmas, he would travel north himself in the spring and find Solomon’s friends in Saratoga with his own eyes. He would not rest, he said, until the thing was done, and he would stay in the neighbourhood until he knew that Solomon was safe. They shook hands in the lamplight, two men of different countries and different colours, joined in a pact of trust.

At last the new house was finished, the last board nailed and the last wall plastered, and Bass packed his tools and said goodbye in the ordinary way of a hired workman. He promised to return before Christmas with news, and Solomon watched the tall figure grow small along the road until the trees closed round it. Then he turned back to the cotton, with a secret that he could tell to no one.

The picking season began again, and with each sack that he filled Solomon silently counted the weeks, trying to work out how long a letter might take to reach New York and how soon an answer might come back. The sums were uncertain, for he knew nothing of the roads and rivers that lay between Marksville and Saratoga, and every week without news seemed longer than the one before.
