He told himself to be patient, but patience was a skill he had already spent years learning.

Far to the north, in Saratoga, the letter reached Parker and Perry, who read it twice over in astonishment, for they had long believed that their old friend had disappeared for ever. They remembered him well, and they knew at once that the news must not be kept from his family for a single hour. They put on their hats, hurried through the cold streets and took the letter straight to Anne.

Anne read the letter standing up, with the children crowding round, and for a moment none of them could speak. After so many years of silence and uncertainty, they learned that Solomon was alive, that he was held in Louisiana as a slave and that he needed their help. They wept for joy and for fear together, knowing that the news was a beginning and not yet a rescue.

Anne carried the letter to Henry B Northup, a lawyer at Sandy Hill, whose family had once owned Solomon’s father and who had known Solomon himself as a boy. He read the letter twice, listened to what Anne had to say and agreed at once to do everything that the law allowed. He was a methodical man, and he began to make a list of the steps that would have to be taken.

Henry studied the statute books and found an act of 1840 for the protection of free citizens, which allowed the governor of New York to appoint an agent to bring home any person kidnapped and sold into slavery. It was a rare piece of law, and he was glad that someone had thought of the need. But it demanded proof of every claim that was made, and proof meant a great deal of patient and tedious work.

Henry went from door to door in Saratoga and the villages around it, collecting sworn statements from Solomon’s neighbours, employers and friends, each of whom declared that he had been born free and had lived quietly among them for years. The papers piled up on his desk, one signature after another, until the evidence was beyond dispute. It was a quiet and touching tribute to a man whose name had almost been forgotten.

Henry carried the statements to Albany, where Governor Washington Hunt studied them with care and then signed an order giving Henry official authority to travel to Louisiana and bring Solomon home. Winter was already setting in, and Henry, who knew that every day could matter, began at once to prepare for the long journey south. He did not yet know the name of the planter, nor the way to the plantation.

In Louisiana Christmas came with its three days of freedom, its supper and its dancing, but Bass did not appear, and the promised news did not arrive. Solomon played the violin with an aching heart, glancing at the road every few minutes in the hope of seeing a figure on it, while the others danced around him in their best clothes. The music was cheerful and the dancing was lively, but the man who played it had never felt further from home.

Christmas passed without a word from anywhere, and in the cold, grey days of the new year Solomon returned to the cotton field almost without hope, picking mechanically and avoiding the eyes of the others. He wondered whether Bass had forgotten him, whether the letter had been lost or whether the friends in Saratoga had long ago ceased to care. He could not know that, a thousand miles away, a carriage was already on its way.

Henry set out from the snowy north with his papers in a leather bag, travelling by train through the same towns that Solomon had passed, so full of hope, eleven years before. His first stop was Washington, where he asked for help from men in authority and where, to his relief, he was given letters that would open doors in the South. He understood already that the success of his mission would depend upon the goodwill of strangers.

From Washington Henry travelled on by train and then by steamboat down the broad, slow Mississippi, a long journey in the depths of winter, with cold mist on the water and cotton bales stacked along the decks. He spent the hours in his cabin going over his papers, rehearsing the arguments that he would use and the questions that he might be asked. At every landing he wondered what he would find at the end of the road.

At New Orleans Henry asked the way to Bayou Boeuf, a name that few people knew, and after several inquiries he was told that he must first go to Marksville, the seat of the parish. He wrote the name on the first page of his notebook and underlined it twice. It was the nearest thing to a destination that he had yet been given, and it was still a long way off.

Henry went on by a small steamer up the Red River, through cypress swamps and cotton fields and past landing stages where bales were piled like walls. He reflected that Solomon himself had once been carried along the very same river as a captive, and the thought turned his anxiety into a quiet anger and a stronger determination. He was beginning to see, with painful clarity, how many miles lay between a free man’s home and a slave’s grave.

At Marksville Henry met a local lawyer named John P Waddill, a man who understood how the courts of the parish worked and who listened gravely to the story that Henry laid before him. After reading the papers from New York, he agreed to help in any way that he could. It was a stroke of luck that Henry had not dared to count on, and it saved him weeks of anxious searching.

Waddill explained that Louisiana law was framed to protect owners, and that Henry would have to prove, in proper legal form, that Solomon was a free man wrongly held. Force would only make matters worse, he warned, and it might even endanger Solomon himself. The work must be done through the court, step by step, and with a cool head.

Waddill drew up a petition in proper legal form, asking the court to order the sheriff to take Solomon from Epps and bring him before a judge. He supported it with the papers that Henry had brought from New York, and the judge read the evidence, was satisfied that the case was serious, and signed the order. A piece of paper that Solomon could not see had suddenly become his best protection.

Early the next morning the sheriff and Henry climbed into a carriage with the court’s order in an envelope and set out for Bayou Boeuf, the sheriff sitting upright and silent and Henry staring ahead at the road. Henry had decided that he would try to find Solomon quietly in the field, rather than make his first call at the house, and thereby give Epps no time to hide his property or prepare his defence. It was a simple plan, and everything that mattered to Solomon depended upon its working as they hoped.

The carriage rolled slowly along the muddy road beside the bayou, past plantation after plantation, while the sheriff asked the way of the few people that they met. At last they came to the edge of Epps’s land, and Henry saw in the distance a line of workers bent over the cotton rows, with the white fields stretching away behind them. He leaned forward in his seat, and his heart began to beat very fast.

On the morning of the third of January 1853 the carriage drew up by the roadside, and Henry and the sheriff stepped down into the dust and began to walk across the field. A short distance ahead, among the cotton plants, a man was picking steadily with his head down, and he did not look up. He had spent about ten years on that plantation, and he did not yet know that his life was about to change.

Two strangers came walking across the cotton field towards the workers, their boots sinking into the soft earth, and the other pickers glanced up and then bent hastily to their work. Solomon, who had learned long ago that it was dangerous to stare at white visitors, went on picking steadily and did not look up. Visitors came often, and he saw no reason why these two should be any different.

One of the strangers stopped beside him and asked his name, and Solomon, as he had done ten thousand times before, answered that it was Platt, the name that had been given to him in the pens of New Orleans. The man looked at him closely, and then he asked, very quietly, whether he knew who the stranger was. Solomon straightened his back and looked into the face, and something that had been asleep inside him for twelve years woke with a jolt.

Solomon suddenly knew the man, who was none other than Henry B Northup, the lawyer from Sandy Hill, and he felt his legs shake beneath him. Henry stretched out his hand and called him by his true name, Solomon Northup, which nobody had spoken aloud in that field for twelve years, and for a moment he could not answer. Then he took the hand in both of his own and wept, and the cotton sack slid from his shoulder to the ground.

Epps came hurrying out from the house, red in the face, and demanded to know what the strangers wanted with his property. The sheriff stepped forward, calmly produced the court’s order and informed him that the man he called Platt was a free citizen of New York named Solomon Northup, who had been wrongfully held. For the first time in ten years, Solomon saw the planter lost for words.

Epps raged and swore that he had bought Platt honestly, that he had paid a good sum for him and that he would not give him up to anybody. But the law was plain, the sheriff stood firm and Henry quietly named the people in New York who would swear to Solomon’s freedom, and in the end there was nothing that the planter could do to stop them. He turned away in silence, a man who had lost both his property and his dignity in a single morning.

Solomon was told that he might go at once, and he hurried to the cabin to gather what he owned, a few old clothes and the violin that he had played for so many years. His hands shook as he tied the bundle, and he could hardly believe that this was not a dream from which he would wake in the dark with the horn calling him to the field. When he came out again into the sunlight, the carriage was still waiting at the roadside, and it was no dream.

Patsey came running from the cabins, weeping aloud, and threw her arms about him, and for a moment she would not let him go. Epps ordered her back in a harsh voice, and Solomon, who had saved no one and been saved himself, could do nothing but gently free himself from her grasp. It was the most painful moment of that day, and he never forgot it.

The others stood in a silent group in front of the cabins, Uncle Abram, Aunt Phebe and the rest, and some of them called out blessings as Solomon climbed into the carriage. None of them could follow, and he knew, with a pain that went through him like a blade, that he would never see any of them again. He had come among them as a stranger, and he left them as brothers and sisters.

Epps stood at the gate shouting angrily as the carriage turned onto the road, while the sheriff looked straight ahead. Solomon looked back until the cotton fields, the cabins and the great new house had disappeared behind the trees, and he could still hear the voices of the people he had left behind. He had spent ten years in that place, and he was leaving it at the speed of a trotting horse.

In the small courthouse at Marksville the judge heard the evidence, read the sworn statements from Saratoga and listened to Solomon’s plain account of what had happened to him. Then he declared that Solomon Northup was a free man who had been wrongfully held, and the legal papers were completed and signed. At last Solomon held in his hands a paper that no one could take away, and it had taken twelve years, a patient carpenter from Canada and a stubborn lawyer from New York to put it there.

Solomon and Henry went down the Red River and then the Mississippi by steamboat, and for the first time in twelve years Solomon travelled as a free passenger, standing at the rail with the cold wind in his face. Nobody held a whip over him, shouted an order or asked him for a pass. He felt strangely light, as though he had set down a heavy load and had not yet learned how to walk without it.

In New Orleans Solomon walked through the streets where he had once been exposed for sale, past the warehouses and the slave pens and the very wharf where the Orleans had landed him in chains twelve years before. He looked at it all as a free man with a lawyer at his side and a certificate in his pocket, and he found that the city had somehow shrunk. It could no longer make him afraid, though it would never stop making him angry.

In Washington Henry and Solomon went looking for James Burch, the dealer who had held Solomon in the pen beneath the dome of the Capitol, and they found him still doing business in the capital. Burch was arrested and charged with kidnapping, and for a brief moment it seemed that justice might have a chance in the capital of the free republic. Solomon had waited twelve years to see him standing in front of a judge.

In court Burch claimed that he had bought Solomon in good faith, and the case turned on whose word the court would believe. Since the courts of that time would not accept the word of a black man against that of a white man, the case collapsed and Burch walked free. Solomon watched the outcome with fury and with a weary understanding of what the law was worth.

From Washington they went north by train, through towns and fields white with winter snow, and Solomon sat beside the window and watched the country slide past. He had not been home for twelve years, and he found that he could think of nothing else: the faces of his wife and children, the sound of the hotel bells, the smell of woodsmoke in a New York street. Every mile brought him nearer to the people he had thought he might never see.

In January 1853 Solomon came home to his family, and when he reached the door, Anne and the children were waiting for him, and for a long time nobody could speak. The little ones he had left were grown, and his daughter Margaret held in her arms a baby boy who had been named Solomon Northup in his honour. Solomon, who had once been told that he was nobody, held the child and wept for happiness.

Little by little Solomon learned what had happened while he was away: his mother had died, his children had grown into adults with lives of their own and many of his old friends had given him up for lost. He felt both a deep joy at what had been preserved and a deep sorrow at all that had been taken, and he knew that he would never be able to give back the years. Yet he was home, and for the first time in twelve years he could walk along any road he chose without asking leave.

With the help of a writer named David Wilson, Solomon told his story from beginning to end, and Wilson put it into order and checked what he could against the facts. Solomon insisted that every word be true, and that nothing be added for effect. He dedicated the finished book to Harriet Beecher Stowe, whose novel against slavery had moved so many readers only a year earlier.

Published in 1853, the book sold many thousands of copies, was praised in the newspapers and made many readers ask hard questions about slavery. Solomon travelled to meetings in the northern states to tell his story, and he tried to bring the men who had tricked him to court, but the cases ended without a conviction and none of them was ever punished. Little is known of the end of his life, for he was last heard of in about 1857, and no record of his death has been found.

Slavery in the United States ended only in 1865, but the book that Solomon Northup left behind is still read around the world, in dozens of languages, as one of the clearest first-hand accounts of slavery ever written. It reminds us that freedom is not a gift that one person may give or take from another, and that the courage of a single man, together with the kindness of a few others, can change a life. Solomon Northup came home, and by telling his story so plainly, he left the rest of us a duty to remember.
